genres.definition: Acid house is house with a Roland TB-303 bass sequence as the lead element: its resonant filter, accent and slide are swept in real time over a swung house drum pattern at 118–126 BPM. It came out of Chicago in 1985–1987 (Phuture's "Acid Tracks") and fuelled the UK's 1988 "second summer of love" rave boom. The squelching, modulating 303 line is the whole identity; harmony and vocals are minimal.
genres.name: Acid House

genres.definition: Acid jazz is the late-1980s and 1990s London club movement that revived 1970s jazz-funk and soul-jazz as dance music for DJ culture: live bands and producers playing or sampling Rhodes-and-wah grooves at 95–115 BPM with soul-pop vocals or rap verses, hip-hop and house references and modern production. Named by DJs Gilles Peterson and Chris Bangs around 1987 and carried by Acid Jazz Records and Talkin' Loud, it produced the Brand New Heavies, Jamiroquai, Incognito, Galliano, the Young Disciples, Us3 and the James Taylor Quartet, then dissolved into nu-jazz, neo-soul and broken beat by the late 1990s. It is filed under jazz because its idiom is jazz-funk; its production is club music.
genres.name: Acid Jazz

genres.definition: Acid techno is techno whose lead element is a Roland TB-303 (or clone) line: a squelching, resonant-filter bass-lead that runs through most of the track. It took the 303 from Chicago acid-house, put it over harder, faster, straighter techno drums and, in its 1990s London form (Stay Up Forever, Liberator DJs), became the sound of the UK free-party and squat scene. Modern techno uses acid lines constantly; the note applies when the 303 is the defining carrier, not a passing hook.
genres.name: Acid Techno

genres.definition: Acid trance is trance whose lead voice is a TB-303 line, with resonance and cutoff swept through the track, placed inside a trance arrangement of pads, chord changes and a kick-less breakdown at roughly 135–142 BPM. It formed in Frankfurt around 1992 (Harthouse, Hardfloor's "Acperience 1") and in Belgium and the UK (Bonzai, Platipus), peaked in the mid-1990s and was revived around 1998–2002 by Kai Tracid and A*S*Y*S. Where acid-techno is a 303 jam over techno drums, acid trance gives the 303 a song-like trance frame.
genres.name: Acid Trance

genres.definition: Acidcore is the acid-led strand of free-tekno: distorted, often layered 303 sequences dominating a 160–180 BPM distorted kick with a tekno bass bounce, developed slowly over long filter sweeps, dark and hookless. It takes the 303 obsession of UK acid-techno to free-party tempi and saturation. The term is a scene label used on teknival and free-party line-ups rather than a store category; its edges toward "mental tekno" and hardtek are soft.
genres.name: Acidcore

genres.definition: Adult contemporary is the ballad-leaning, melody-first strand of pop defined by a radio format and chart rather than by a scene: soft, polished songs for adult listeners, built on piano or pads, a restrained rhythm section and an emotive lead vocal that climbs to a belted final chorus. It grew out of easy listening in the 1960s (the Billboard chart took the name in 1979) and splits into soft AC (ballads, older catalogue) and hot AC (brisker recent hits). Power ballads of the 1980s–1990s are its centre of gravity.
genres.name: Adult Contemporary

genres.definition: African groups the popular and traditional musics of sub-Saharan Africa and its direct diaspora output: highlife and juju (Ghana, Nigeria), Afrobeat (Fela Kuti), Congolese rumba and soukous, mbaqanga, kwaito, gqom and amapiano (South Africa), benga (Kenya), mbalax (Senegal), kuduro (Angola), Malian desert blues and griot traditions, Ethio-jazz, and the 2010s–2020s Afrobeats pop wave from Lagos and Accra. Common ground: polyrhythm built on bell or shaker cycles, interlocking melodic lines, call and response and dance function. North African and Arabic-influenced styles are filed under world-regional.
genres.name: African

genres.definition: Afro-Cuban jazz is the Cuban strand of latin-jazz: bebop and big-band jazz improvisation over son clave, tumbao bass, piano montuno and the conga–bongo–timbales battery. It was created in 1940s New York by Machito's Afro-Cubans under Mario Bauzá and by Dizzy Gillespie with Chano Pozo ("Cubop"), fuelled the mambo era at the Palladium, and has been renewed by Cuban musicians from Cachao's descargas to Irakere and the players who left Cuba from the 1980s onward. The clave is the organising principle; the solos are jazz.
genres.name: Afro-Cuban Jazz

genres.definition: Afro house is house at 120–125 BPM whose groove rests on layered African hand percussion, chanted or sung vocals in African languages, kalimba or marimba lines and a warm minor or modal chord bed under a four-on-the-floor kick. It consolidated in South Africa in the 2000s (Black Coffee, Culoe De Song, Soulistic Music) out of kwaito and imported soulful-house, with a parallel Angolan and Lisbon strand, and became a global club and Beatport category in the late 2010s and 2020s. Afro tech is its darker, drier, synth-led edge toward melodic techno.
genres.name: Afro House

genres.definition: Alternative hip-hop is the umbrella for hip-hop that sits outside the mainstream conventions of its era in production, song form or persona: eclectic and non-canonical samples, live instruments, jazz and psychedelic textures, irregular structures, humour and introspection. It is defined by difference from the centre rather than by one sound; the Native Tongues of 1989–1993, the Rawkus and Definitive Jux underground of the late 1990s, Stones Throw, Anticon and Odd Future belong to it at different times. Jazz rap is its best-defined sub-style.
genres.name: Alternative Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Amapiano is South African house at 110–115 BPM in which a log-drum bass, a pitched percussive bass pattern off the kick grid, carries the pulse under jazzy piano chords, shaker loops and sung or chanted vocals, with a soft or absent kick and long piano intros. It formed in the Gauteng townships around Pretoria and Johannesburg in the mid-2010s out of deep-house, kwaito and jazz, broke nationally with Kabza De Small and DJ Maphorisa in 2019 and went global during 2020–2023. The name is isiZulu for "the pianos".
genres.name: Amapiano

genres.definition: Ambient is the beatless core of ambient-downtempo: music built from sustained tones, slow harmonic motion and space, meant to sit in a room as texture rather than demand attention. Brian Eno named it in the mid-1970s; its material ranges from synth pads and tape loops to processed piano, field recordings and voice. There is no kick, no meter and no phrase grid; duration and timbre carry the piece.
genres.name: Ambient

genres.definition: Ambient and downtempo is the listening end of electronic music: texture-first tracks with no steady dance kick, either beatless (ambient, drone) or built on slow beats under 110 BPM (downtempo, trip-hop, chill-out). It runs from Brian Eno's 1970s ambient through the 1990s chill-out room and Bristol trip-hop to 2010s lo-fi and ambient techno. Space, duration and timbre carry the music; rhythm is optional.
genres.name: Ambient & Downtempo

genres.definition: Ambient techno is techno turned down for listening: a quiet, often muffled 4/4 kick or soft break at roughly 118–130 BPM under sustained pads, Detroit-style chords and bleeps, with long beatless passages. It formed in the UK and US around 1989–1993 (The Orb's ambient house, Warp's "Artificial Intelligence", Aphex Twin, B12, Pete Namlook's FAX label) and found a second canon in GAS and Kompakt's Pop Ambient series. It keeps techno's steady grid where ambient has none and IDM breaks it.
genres.name: Ambient Techno

genres.definition: Art pop is pop that treats the song as an art object: pop form, vocal focus and length kept, but with conceptual framing, unconventional structures, mixed acoustic-electronic palettes and studio manipulation as composition. It emerged in the mid-1960s UK and US out of art-school thinking (Warhol and the Velvet Underground, Richard Hamilton's influence on Roxy Music) and runs from Brian Wilson, Bowie and Roxy Music through Kate Bush and Grace Jones to Björk, Grimes, FKA twigs and Julia Holter. It has no fixed sound and no single peak; it is identified by what the production does to pop, not by a palette.
genres.name: Art Pop

genres.definition: Art rock is rock made with an art-school or avant-garde stance: song-length pieces that keep a rhythm section and a sung lead but treat timbre, production, structure and lyric as experimental material. The Velvet Underground, David Bowie, Roxy Music, Brian Eno, Talking Heads, Kate Bush, Peter Gabriel and later Radiohead are the usual examples. It overlaps progressive-rock (which goes long and virtuosic), glam-rock (which goes theatrical and simple) and new-wave (which goes tight and danceable); art-pop is the same stance applied to pop rather than rock instrumentation. The label is a critical category more than a scene, so its boundaries are soft.
genres.name: Art Rock

genres.definition: Atmospheric black metal is black-metal stretched into long, repetitive, reverb-washed tracks with synth pads, acoustic or ambient interludes and a buried vocal, aimed at immersion rather than aggression. Burzum's "Filosofem" (1996) and Summoning's keyboard-led epics are the usual starting points; Wolves in the Throne Room and the Pacific Northwest ("Cascadian") scene, Drudkh, Paysage d'Hiver, Agalloch and Saor carry it through the 2000s and 2010s. It borders blackgaze (brighter, shoegaze chords, clean vocals) and post-metal (no blasts, no shrieks).
genres.name: Atmospheric Black Metal

genres.definition: Atmospheric drum and bass is the pad-led, ambient and jazz-inflected strand of drum-and-bass that formed in London in 1993–1997 around LTJ Bukem's Good Looking Records: rolling, lightly chopped breaks at 160–172 BPM mixed under long chord washes, Detroit-style stabs and a soft sub holding notes for bars at a time. It was marketed as "intelligent" drum and bass at the time and is the direct ancestor of liquid. Pads louder than drums and the absence of a hard drop are the identifiers.
genres.name: Atmospheric Drum and Bass

genres.definition: Avant-garde jazz is the composition-minded strand that grew out of free-jazz: musicians who keep improvisation central but frame it with written themes, sectional forms, graphic or game scores, unconventional instruments, electronics and theatre. Its institutions are the AACM in Chicago (1965), the Black Artists Group in St. Louis, the New York loft and Downtown scenes and the Dutch Instant Composers Pool; its figures include Anthony Braxton, the Art Ensemble of Chicago, Sun Ra, Henry Threadgill, John Zorn and Misha Mengelberg. In common use "avant-garde" and "free" overlap; this atlas splits them by structure, not by date.
genres.name: Avant-Garde Jazz

genres.definition: Balearic beat is a DJ sound rather than a production style, filed under ambient-downtempo for its tempo and function: the eclectic mid-tempo mix of pop, disco, Italo, early house and guitar ballads that DJ Alfredo played at Amnesia, Ibiza, in the mid-1980s and that London DJs imported in 1987–1988. Records run roughly 90–120 BPM, lean warm and major, and span band production to electronic. "Nu-Balearic" from the 2000s names new productions made for that sunset slot.
genres.name: Balearic Beat

genres.definition: Baltimore club is the Baltimore form of breakbeat dance music: a fixed, syncopated 808 kick cell at 128–135 BPM under a looped Think or Sing Sing break, with a one-beat vocal chop repeated every bar and shouted call-and-response as the hook. It formed in the late 1980s and early 1990s from house, hip-hop and Miami bass and is the parent of Jersey club and Philly club. A repeating kick cell plus a break loop plus a one-beat vocal chop are the identifiers.
genres.name: Baltimore Club

genres.definition: Baroque pop is the 1960s form of chamber-pop: rock-era pop songs dressed in harpsichord, string quartet, oboe and French horn, with Baroque-derived figures (descending bass lines, suspensions, counterpoint) under stacked vocal harmonies. It emerged in the mid-1960s — the Zombies' "She's Not There" (1964) is cited as a starting point, the Left Banke's "Walk Away Renée" (1966) as the first recognisable single — and peaked with *Pet Sounds*, "Eleanor Rigby" and "A Whiter Shade of Pale" before fading in the 1970s. Chamber pop revived its spirit from the 1990s on.
genres.name: Baroque Pop

genres.definition: Bass house is 2010s house at 125–128 BPM whose drop is carried by a heavy, modulated synth bass (growl, wobble, formant or reese) over a wide sub, with shuffled garage-style percussion, chopped rap or ragga vocal samples and a build-and-drop arrangement. It formed in the UK around 2012–2014 where jackin' house met bassline, UK garage and dubstep wobble (Hannah Wants, Chris Lorenzo, My Nu Leng, Jack Beats), and was fixed as a category by AC Slater's Night Bass (Los Angeles, 2014) and Jauz's "Feel the Volume" (2015). The bass is the hook; everything else is set-up.
genres.name: Bass House

genres.definition: Bassline is the northern English four-on-the-floor strand of uk-garage: a kick on every beat at 138–142 BPM, a bouncing, pitch-bent mid-range bass riff as the hook, and chopped pop or R&B vocal hooks. It grew out of speed garage and 4x4 garage played at Sheffield's Niche club in the early 2000s, charted in 2007–2008, and returned in a 2010s revival that overlaps with bass house. The bass riff is the melody.
genres.name: Bassline

genres.definition: Bebop is the small-group jazz of the 1940s that moved the music from the dance floor to the listening room: fast tempos, chromatic 1/8-note improvisation over dense ii–V harmony, angular unison heads written on the chord changes of standards, and a rhythm section in which the ride cymbal keeps time while the bass drum drops irregular accents. Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, Kenny Clarke and Max Roach defined it in New York between about 1941 and 1950; its vocabulary is the basis of most jazz improvisation since.
genres.name: Bebop

genres.definition: Bedroom pop is the 2010s DIY form of indie-pop: songs written, recorded and mixed alone on a laptop, with programmed or sampled drums, cheap keyboards or clean guitar, a quiet close-miked vocal and deliberate lo-fi treatment (roll-off, hiss, wobble), released independently on SoundCloud, YouTube and Bandcamp. Clairo's "Pretty Girl" (2017), Rex Orange County, Cuco, girl in red, beabadoobee and mxmtoon are the reference acts. The term borrows from the lo-fi tradition that runs from 1980s home recording through chillwave and lo-fi hip-hop; the production constraint is the aesthetic.
genres.name: Bedroom Pop

genres.definition: Berlin School is the 1970s West Berlin strand of ambient electronics built on analog step sequencers: a looping bass or arpeggio pattern runs for minutes under Mellotron pads and improvised synth leads, with no drum kit. Tangerine Dream's "Phaedra" (1974) and Klaus Schulze's mid-1970s albums define it. Where ambient is beatless, Berlin School has a pulse but no beat, and its side-long pieces are the ancestor of trance and ambient techno sequencing.
genres.name: Berlin School

genres.definition: Big band is the large-ensemble format of jazz: ten to eighteen players in saxophone, trumpet and trombone sections plus a rhythm section, playing written arrangements with call and response, block-chord voicings and a shout chorus, with solo spots cut into the chart. It grew out of 1920s dance orchestras, became the vehicle of the swing era and has continued since 1946 as a concert and repertory format that also plays bebop, Latin and modern material. The note is filed under swing because the format's sound is defined by that era; the format is an instrumentation, not a feel.
genres.name: Big Band

genres.definition: Big beat is the 1995–1999 British strand of breakbeat that put compressed, overdriven funk and rock breaks under guitar riffs, acid lines, rave stabs and shouted vocal hooks at 110–125 BPM, arranged like songs rather than DJ tools. It came out of Brighton's Big Beat Boutique and London's Heavenly Social and reached the charts through The Chemical Brothers, Fatboy Slim and The Prodigy. Loud sampled breaks plus rock samples plus a sung or shouted hook are the identifiers.
genres.name: Big Beat

genres.definition: Birmingham techno is the dry, grey, loop-based techno that Regis, Surgeon and Female built around the Downwards label and the House of God club night from 1993: hard 909 kicks without reverb, metallic percussion loops, EBM-style bass pulses and no melody, at 132–140 BPM. It is the direct ancestor of 2010s industrial-techno and a template for dark-techno, but it is drier, thinner and more industrial-tinged than either.
genres.name: Birmingham Techno

genres.definition: Black metal is the cold, treble-heavy extreme branch of metal: tremolo-picked minor-key riffs, blast beats, a shrieked high vocal, deliberately raw production and occult, anti-Christian or misanthropic themes. The first wave (Venom, Bathory, Hellhammer, Mercyful Fate, 1982–1987) is fast thrash-metal and speed-metal with satanic imagery; the second wave in Norway (Mayhem, Darkthrone, Burzum, Emperor, Immortal, 1991–1994) fixed the sound described here. atmospheric-black-metal, symphonic-metal's black strand and pagan folk-metal branch from it.
genres.name: Black Metal

genres.definition: Blackgaze is atmospheric-black-metal played with shoegaze and post-rock harmony: blast beats and shrieks under bright, consonant, reverb-washed major and suspended chords, with clean sung passages and quiet-loud crescendos. Alcest's "Souvenirs d'un autre monde" (2007) is the usual origin; Deafheaven's "Sunbather" (2013) brought it to a wide audience. The darker, more dissonant end shades back into black-metal; the end without blasts shades into post-metal.
genres.name: Blackgaze

genres.definition: Bleep techno is the first British techno strand: sparse drum-machine tracks from Sheffield, Leeds and Bradford (1989–1991) built on two things, a very deep sub bass taken from reggae sound systems and short high-pitched "bleep" motifs, with hip-hop swing and little else in between. Warp Records was founded on it. It fed British rave and, through its reduction and humour, the later wonky-techno and much of Warp's electronica.
genres.name: Bleep Techno

genres.definition: Blues is African-American song music from the Deep South built on a repeating 12-bar I–IV–V cycle, a vocal line answered by guitar or harmonica, blue-note melody and a shuffle or triplet feel. It formed around 1900 and fed rock and roll, jazz, R&B and soul directly. Branches: Delta and country blues, Piedmont, Texas, jump blues and boogie-woogie, Chicago electric blues, blues rock, soul blues and contemporary blues. The 12-bar form and the blues scale hold across all of them.
genres.name: Blues

genres.definition: Boogie is the post-disco form of disco from roughly 1979 to 1985: slower (100–118 BPM), stripped of orchestral strings, built on drum machines or tight drums with handclaps, a prominent syncopated synth bass and funk guitar, with soulful sung leads. It is the sound of New York's Prelude and West End labels, Los Angeles' SOLAR roster and UK Brit-funk, named retrospectively by collectors. It sits between disco, funk and the electro and house that followed.
genres.name: Boogie

genres.definition: Boogie-woogie is piano blues built on a repeating left-hand ostinato of eight notes to the bar under improvised right-hand riffs, played fast and percussively over the 12-bar cycle. It grew in Texas and Louisiana work camps and Chicago house parties, was first recorded in the 1920s (Jimmy Blythe, Meade Lux Lewis, Pine Top Smith, Cow Cow Davenport) and became a national craze after the 1938 "From Spirituals to Swing" concert put Albert Ammons, Pete Johnson and Meade Lux Lewis on stage at Carnegie Hall. Its bass figures became the engine of jump-blues, of rock-and-roll piano and of the guitar boogie of John Lee Hooker and ZZ Top.
genres.name: Boogie-Woogie

genres.definition: Boom bap is the sample-based drum style of hip-hop: a punchy sampled kick ("boom") and a hard, dry snare ("bap") chopped from funk and soul breaks and re-sequenced on an SP-1200 or MPC, under a 2- or 4-bar loop and a dense rap flow, at 85–95 BPM. It is the default sound of late-1980s and 1990s New York hip-hop and the reference point that later styles are measured against. The name describes the drums; the style is the drums plus the loop.
genres.name: Boom Bap

genres.definition: Bounce is the New Orleans form of southern-hip-hop: fast call-and-response chants, roll calls and dance commands over a near-constant 1-bar loop, almost always the "Triggerman" drum and bell pattern from The Showboys' "Drag Rap" (1986) or the "Brown Beat" from Derek B's "Rock the Beat", at roughly 96–104 BPM. It formed in 1991 and has stayed a local dance music with national flares (Cash Money's late-1990s hits, Big Freedia and "sissy bounce" in the 2010s, pop samples since). It is defined by the loop and the chant, not by verses.
genres.name: Bounce

genres.definition: Bouncy techno is the Scottish 1990s form of accessible gabber: 160–172 BPM, a distorted kick with a tuned bass stab on every offbeat (the "bounce"), simple bright hooks and rave stabs, popularised by Scott Brown (Bass X, Evolution Records), Ultra-Sonic and the Rezerection events, and also played in the Netherlands and Germany. Despite the name it is hard-dance rather than techno; its offbeat bass is the ancestor of the jumpstyle and hard-dance bounce, and it is a frequent false match for hard-techno and schranz at similar tempi.
genres.name: Bouncy Techno

genres.definition: Breakbeat is electronic dance music built on sampled or programmed broken drum patterns at 105–150 BPM with a full-tempo feel: the snare falls on 2 and 4 at the notated tempo and the bass does not drop to half-time. It covers UK breakbeat hardcore (1990–1993), big beat (1995–1999), nu-skool breaks (1998–2008) and Florida breaks, and it is the parent lineage of drum and bass. The groove comes from the sampled drummer's swing and from chopped, resequenced hits.
genres.name: Breakbeat

genres.definition: Breakcore is the broken-beat wing of hardcore: chopped and mangled sampled breaks at 160–220 BPM (unstable), distorted gabber kicks dropped into the pattern, ragga, cartoon and pop samples and a structure that breaks the DJ phrase grid. It formed in the late 1990s where jungle, gabber, digital-hardcore and idm overlapped in Berlin, London and the Netherlands and peaked in the mid-2000s around Planet Mu and Ad Noiseam. Extreme break editing plus gabber kicks plus an unstable grid is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Breakcore

genres.definition: British blues is the blues revival played by British bands from the late 1950s to about 1970: chicago-blues and electric-blues repertoire re-recorded with louder, higher-gain guitar, a rock-weighted drum kit, electric bass and long solos. Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies' Blues Incorporated, John Mayall's Bluesbreakers, the early Rolling Stones and Yardbirds, Peter Green's Fleetwood Mac, Chicken Shack, Savoy Brown and Ten Years After are its core. It led directly into blues-rock and hard rock (Cream, Led Zeppelin) and sent American blues records back to American audiences.
genres.name: British Blues

genres.definition: Broken techno is techno whose drums are breakbeats: kick and snare in syncopated, jungle- or garage-derived patterns at 130–142 BPM under techno sound design (dark pads, deep sub, filtered noise). It crystallised in the 2010s around Munich's Ilian Tape (Zenker Brothers, Skee Mask), Bristol (Livity Sound, Timedance) and Berlin's post-dubstep producers, and by the 2020s "breaks" sections are standard in techno sets. The kick pattern, not the palette, separates it from the rest of techno.
genres.name: Broken Techno

genres.definition: Brostep is the mid-range-heavy, festival-scale strand of dubstep: the 140 BPM half-time grid kept, but the near-sine sub replaced or joined by distorted growling and screeching bass in the 300 Hz–3 kHz band, a snare-roll build and a drop that is the whole point of the track. It grew from UK wobble in 2008–2009, broke out of Los Angeles in 2010–2012 with Skrillex, and remains the sound US audiences mean by "dubstep". The name began as a UK insult and stuck.
genres.name: Brostep

genres.definition: Brutal death metal is death-metal reduced to weight and speed: guttural vocals below the growl, near-constant blast beats, down-tuned chromatic riffs and slam sections — half-time palm-muted chugs that drop the feel to half tempo. It formed around Suffocation's "Effigy of the Forgotten" (1991) on Long Island, was codified as slam by Internal Bleeding and Devourment in the late 1990s and runs as a large underground scene (Unique Leader, Comatose, Sevared, New Standard Elite). It borders technical-death-metal (Suffocation sits in both), grindcore at the short end and deathcore on the breakdown side.
genres.name: Brutal Death Metal

genres.definition: Bubblegum pop is the late-1960s US strand of pop manufactured for preteens and teens: short, upbeat major-key songs with sing-along choruses, nursery-rhyme melodies and candy-and-dancing lyrics, cut by session players under producers who often invented the band afterwards. Kasenetz-Katz productions and Buddah Records set the template around 1968; TV-cartoon and sitcom acts (The Archies, The Monkees, The Partridge Family) carried it into the early 1970s. The term is also used loosely for later teen pop; this note covers the 1968–1972 sound.
genres.name: Bubblegum Pop

genres.definition: Chamber pop is pop arranged with orchestral instruments as structural layers: strings, horns, woodwinds, vibraphone and piano playing independent lines under an intimate vocal, with a soft live rhythm section and a natural, dynamic mix. The term dates from the mid-1980s and the style took shape as an indie subgenre in the mid-1990s as a reaction against grunge's fuzz and lo-fi recording (Eric Matthews, The High Llamas, Cardinal, The Divine Comedy), then widened in the 2000s (Beirut, Grizzly Bear, The Decemberists, Fleet Foxes). It is the heir of 1960s baroque pop.
genres.name: Chamber Pop

genres.definition: Chicago blues is the amplified band form of blues built by Delta migrants on Chicago's South and West Sides after 1945: electric guitar (often slide), harmonica through a microphone and amp, piano, bass and drums playing the delta-blues repertoire as an ensemble shuffle with stop-time riffs. Chess and Vee-Jay recordings of Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Little Walter, Jimmy Reed, Elmore James and Willie Dixon's songs (1948–1960) define it; the late-1950s West Side sound (Otis Rush, Magic Sam, Buddy Guy) and the Alligator era (1971–) extend it. It is the most copied strand of electric-blues and the model for british-blues.
genres.name: Chicago Blues

genres.definition: Chicago house is the original form of house: drum-machine tracks made in Chicago between roughly 1984 and 1989 for the Warehouse, Music Box and Power Plant crowds and released on Trax and DJ International. A loud 909 or 808 pattern, a one-bar synth bass, a stab or two and a repeated vocal phrase; the raw "jack track" and the gospel-tinged song sit side by side. Every later house strand descends from it, and the name is also used for any modern house that copies the raw, machine-forward template.
genres.name: Chicago House

genres.definition: Chillout is the compilation-era, beat-based mellow strand of ambient-downtempo: soft programmed grooves at roughly 95–110 BPM under Rhodes, guitar, strings and pads, produced for bars, sunsets and chill-out rooms. It was named after the UK rave chill-out rooms of 1989–1990 and commercialised through the Café del Mar, Buddha Bar and similar series from the mid-1990s. It is brighter and more groove-based than ambient, and cleaner and less sample-driven than downtempo or trip-hop.
genres.name: Chillout

genres.definition: Chillwave is lo-fi, nostalgic synth-pop filed under ambient-downtempo: hazy vintage synths, soft drum machines, sampled 1980s pop fragments and reverb-buried vocals at slow-to-moderate tempo, with summer and memory as subject. It was named in July 2009 by the blog Hipster Runoff and peaked in 2009–2011 with Washed Out, Neon Indian, Toro y Moi and Memory Tapes. It is song-based where downtempo is loop-based, and performed where vaporwave is sampled.
genres.name: Chillwave

genres.definition: Chopped and screwed is the Houston DJ remix technique turned style within southern-hip-hop: existing rap records slowed to about 60–70 BPM with every element pitched down, then "chopped" with record-skip repeats, scratches and stop-start effects, and often overlaid with freestyles. DJ Screw developed it on the city's South Side in the early 1990s and sold it on hand-dubbed tapes; after his death in 2000 it became Houston's national signature and, later, the ancestor of slowed-and-reverb edits and phonk's vocal treatment. The source is someone else's track; the style is what the slowdown and the chops do to it.
genres.name: Chopped and Screwed

genres.definition: Classical is the notated art-music tradition of Europe and its global successors, from the Baroque (c. 1600) through the Classical and Romantic periods to 20th- and 21st-century concert music, performed by orchestras, chamber ensembles, soloists, choirs and opera companies from scores, without improvisation. It includes opera, sacred and choral music, symphonies, concertos, chamber music, solo keyboard repertoire, film and game scores written in the idiom, and contemporary concert music up to minimalism and post-minimalism. Tempo is not a defining property; timbre, notation, dynamics and form are.
genres.name: Classical

genres.definition: Complextro is the 2010–2013 strand of electro-house named by Porter Robinson for his own style: 128 BPM electro house whose drop switches between many synth patches within each bar, with glitchy stutters, chiptune and video-game timbres and intricate edits replacing electro house's single sustained riff. Porter Robinson, Wolfgang Gartner, Madeon, Mord Fustang and early Zedd define it; OWSLA and mau5trap released it. By 2014 its producers had moved on to future bass and pop.
genres.name: Complextro

genres.definition: Conscious hip-hop is the strand of hip-hop defined by lyric purpose: social, political and historical commentary, critique of racism and poverty, and self-knowledge or uplift, delivered as rap. It is a content label, not a sound; its 1990s core sits on boom bap and jazz-rap production, its 2000s and 2010s records on neo-soul, live-band and trap beats. "The Message" (1982) and Public Enemy define the political pole; Native Tongues, Common, Black Star and Kendrick Lamar define the reflective one.
genres.name: Conscious Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Contemporary blues is blues recorded since the 1980s with modern production and a guitar-led band that borrows from rock, soul, funk and (since the 2010s) hip-hop: full-range loud masters, effects pedals, verse/chorus songwriting beside the 12-bar cycle, and a festival and awards circuit in place of a regional scene. The Alligator roster, Stevie Ray Vaughan's 1983 revival, Robert Cray, Buddy Guy's 1991 comeback, Keb' Mo', Susan Tedeschi, Gary Clark Jr., Christone "Kingfish" Ingram, Shemekia Copeland and Fantastic Negrito define it; the Grammy contemporary blues category (since 1988, under changing names) and the Blues Music Awards institutionalise it. It is the production-era successor of electric-blues, the guitar-led neighbour of soul-blues and the blues-side neighbour of blues-rock.
genres.name: Contemporary Blues

genres.definition: Cool jazz is the late-1940s and 1950s reaction within jazz to bebop's heat: medium tempos, soft horn tones with little vibrato, even dynamics, arranged counterpoint and relaxed phrasing, often from pianoless or unusually orchestrated small groups. It covers the Miles Davis nonet's Birth of the Cool sessions, the Lennie Tristano school, the Modern Jazz Quartet and the West Coast scene around Gerry Mulligan, Chet Baker, Dave Brubeck and Shorty Rogers. The bebop vocabulary stays; the intensity, volume and tempo come down.
genres.name: Cool Jazz

genres.definition: Country blues is the acoustic, mostly solo form of blues recorded from the mid-1920s: one singer with one guitar (sometimes a second guitar or a rack harmonica) performing 12-bar and looser stanza forms with blue-note bends and speech-like phrasing. It is the umbrella for the regional pre-war styles — delta-blues, piedmont-blues, the East Texas school of Blind Lemon Jefferson and the later-named hill-country-blues — and the source material for the amplified electric-blues band styles that replaced it after 1945.
genres.name: Country Blues

genres.definition: Crossbreed is the deliberate hybrid of hardcore and dark drum and bass: a stable 170–180 BPM, blocks with a distorted four-on-the-floor hardcore kick alternating with blocks of two-step drum and bass drums over a Reese bass, with industrial textures and an intact DJ phrase grid. It was named and formalised by The Outside Agency's Genosha One Seven Five label (2008) and the Rotterdam PRSPCT circle, drawing on industrial-hardcore, darkstep and techstep. Both drum patterns inside one track at a stable 175 is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Crossbreed

genres.definition: Crunk is the early-2000s Atlanta and Memphis form of southern-hip-hop built for clubs: a heavy, often distorted 808 kick, loud claps, dark minor synth or brass stabs and shouted call-and-response chants in place of verses, at a slow felt tempo. Lil Jon & The East Side Boyz made it a national sound in 2002–2004; it fed directly into snap and trap. The word means hyped or wild; the music is chant and kick with little else.
genres.name: Crunk

genres.definition: Dance-pop is pop built for clubs and radio at once: a four-on-the-floor kick at roughly 118–130 BPM, a belted or R&B-inflected vocal that carries the hook, and whatever club production is current — disco and hi-NRG in the 1980s, house in the 1990s, electro and EDM in the 2000s–2010s. It emerged around the early 1980s with Madonna, Kylie Minogue and the Stock Aitken Waterman factory, was rebuilt by Swedish producers in the late 1990s, and remains the default form of chart pop. The vocal chorus is the hook; the beat is borrowed.
genres.name: Dance-Pop

genres.definition: Dancefloor drum and bass is the big-room, hook-led strand of drum-and-bass: 172–176 BPM two-step with a pitched lead melody or sung vocal carried through a loud, bright drop, a trance-style build and a pop-shaped arrangement. It formed in the mid-2000s around Pendulum, RAM Records and Breakbeat Kaos, reached the UK charts in 2011–2014 and is the festival main-stage form of the genre. A melodic or vocal hook in the drop plus a loudness jump above 6 dB are the identifiers.
genres.name: Dancefloor Drum and Bass

genres.definition: Dark ambient is ambient stripped of consolation: beatless low drones, sub rumble, dissonant clusters, metallic resonances and field recordings arranged into a threatening or desolate space. It grew out of 1980s industrial music ("ambient industrial"), was named by Cold Meat Industry's Roger Karmanik in the early 1990s and has Lustmord as its most cited pioneer. The 1990s "isolationism" tag and the 2010s Cryo Chamber catalogue belong to the same lineage.
genres.name: Dark Ambient

genres.definition: Dark disco is gloomy, guitar-touched club music at 112–124 BPM that Beatportal (2020) describes as more dystopian than disco, more melancholic than house and more musical than techno: chugging analog bass, smoky synths, angular guitar, modal melodies and haunting vocals over ebm- and new-beat-style drum machines. The sound draws on italo-disco, new wave, EBM, acid and psychedelic rock; the term itself dates from the late 2010s. Beatport files it as a sub-genre of Indie Dance; Berlin clubs such as Salon zur Wilden Renate, Kater Blau and Mensch Meier are named homes.
genres.name: Dark Disco

genres.definition: Dark techno is the dry, deep, slow-evolving techno that Berghain, Ostgut Ton and Klockworks made the global club default between about 2008 and 2016: a rounded kick and deep sub at 128–134 BPM, sparse grey percussion, occasional dub-washed stabs, no melody, no drops. "Berlin techno" and "Berghain sound" are scene labels for the same thing. It descends from birmingham-techno, dub-techno and loop-techno and sits between hypnotic-techno and industrial-techno without the former's polyrhythms or the latter's noise.
genres.name: Dark Techno

genres.definition: Darkcore is the dark UK strand of 1992–1993 breakbeat hardcore, filed under early-hardcore: 140–160 BPM, chopped sampled breaks over heavy sub bass, time-stretched vocals, horror and sci-fi samples and minor pads, with the rave pianos stripped out. It is the bridge between breakbeat hardcore and jungle and the counterpart of the happy strand that split off at the same time. In continental usage "darkcore" is sometimes applied to dark gabber with horror atmospheres; that material is covered under doomcore and industrial hardcore here.
genres.name: Darkcore

genres.definition: Darkpsy is the fast, lead-less, night-time strand of psytrance: roughly 150–160 BPM, a hard dry kick over a dense rolling bass, no sustained melody, and a thick layer of dissonant stabs, horror samples and fast FX. It consolidated in the early 2000s around Russian, Danish and German producers and labels (Parvati Records, Osom Music) and later split into the slower, organic forest-psytrance and the faster, digital hi-tech-psytrance. It is the psytrance strand closest to techno's pressure-first logic.
genres.name: Darkpsy

genres.definition: Darkstep is the fast, distorted and horror-themed end of techstep: 172–185 BPM two-step with saturated, layered snares, overdriven Reese bass and dense metallic percussion, the drums as loud as the bass. It grew out of late-1990s techstep in Birmingham, Germany and the Netherlands and later fed the drum and bass–hardcore hybrid called crossbreed. Distorted drums at a tempo above the drum and bass centre are the identifiers.
genres.name: Darkstep

genres.definition: Death metal is the extreme branch of metal that pushed thrash-metal past its limits in 1985–1991: guitars tuned down, riffs chromatic and dissonant, drums alternating between blast beats and double-kick runs, and a low growled vocal with no pitch. Tampa (Death, Morbid Angel, Obituary, Deicide), Stockholm (Entombed, Dismember) and the Earache roster (Carcass, Bolt Thrower) define it; it splits into melodic-death-metal, technical-death-metal and brutal-death-metal, overlaps grindcore at the short end and feeds deathcore in the 2000s.
genres.name: Death Metal

genres.definition: Deep dubstep is the original and sparse strand of dubstep: a half-time kick on 1 and snare on 3 at 138–142 BPM, a near-sine sub bass sustained under the bar, dub delays and reverb, and almost nothing in the mid-range. It is the DMZ, Tempa and Deep Medi sound of South London from 2005 onward, named "deep" once wobble and brostep took the word dubstep elsewhere, and revived in the 2010s under the "140" tag. The sub is the lead; everything else is space around it.
genres.name: Deep Dubstep

genres.definition: Deep house is the slow, chord-led, low-key strand of house: 118–124 BPM, a soft kick, sustained jazz-voiced chords and pads, a warm bass and sparse vocals. It began with Larry Heard's Mr. Fingers records in Chicago in 1985–1986 and was shaped in the 1990s by New York and New Jersey producers around Kerri Chandler and by Detroit's Moodymann and Theo Parrish. The 2010s saw the name attached to a chart-pop sound that this atlas files under tropical-house and future-house; this note describes the original.
genres.name: Deep House

genres.definition: Delta blues is the country-blues of the Mississippi Delta, the flood plain between the Mississippi and Yazoo rivers: solo voice and guitar with bottleneck slide in open tunings, a hammering thumb bass, repeating riffs instead of strummed chords and an intense, often shouted vocal. Recorded from the late 1920s (Charley Patton, Son House, Tommy Johnson, Skip James, Robert Johnson), it is the direct ancestor of chicago-blues through the post-war migration of Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Elmore James.
genres.name: Delta Blues

genres.definition: Detroit techno is the founding strand of techno: four-on-the-floor drum-machine music made in Detroit from the mid-1980s by Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson and the second wave around Underground Resistance, Carl Craig and Jeff Mills. Compared with later European techno it is more harmonic and more funk-rooted: jazz-voiced chords, melodic leads and swung percussion over a dry 909 kick.
genres.name: Detroit Techno

genres.definition: Digital hardcore is hardcore techno and jungle drums fused with punk: shouted political vocals, distorted guitar riffs and song form over gabber kicks and sped-up breaks at 170–200 BPM. It was named after Alec Empire's Digital Hardcore Recordings (Berlin, 1994) and defined by Atari Teenage Riot in 1992–1999; it fed early breakcore and the noise-punk fringe. Shouted punk vocals for most of the track over hardcore drums is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Digital Hardcore

genres.definition: Disco house is house whose hook is a sampled 1970s disco or funk phrase: a 2–4-bar loop of strings, horns, guitar, bass and vocal, laid under a 909 kick and clap at 122–128 BPM and arranged by cutting and restoring the loop. It grew out of Chicago's sample-based 1990s house (Cajual, Relief, DJ Sneak, Derrick Carter) and New York (Kenny Dope, Henry Street Music) and peaked in 1996–2000 alongside its filter-heavy Paris cousin, french-house. The record is the sample plus the kick; everything else is editing.
genres.name: Disco House

genres.definition: Disco and nu-disco covers four-on-the-floor dance music at 100–128 BPM with a played or emulated band palette: strings, horns, octave or slap bass, funk guitar, an offbeat open hat and full sung vocals. Classic disco (1973–1980) is band music that DJs extended into 12-inch mixes; Italo disco, space disco, disco house and nu-disco (2000s–) rebuild it with synthesisers, samplers and machine drums. It is the direct ancestor of house and sits inside electronic because the DJ edit, the extended mix and the drum machine arrived through it.
genres.name: Disco & Nu-Disco

genres.definition: Donk (also scouse house or UK bounce) is a bouncy strand of UK hard-house from North West England: banging kicks at 150–160 BPM, a hollow, plucked offbeat bass stab that literally goes "donk", fast snare rolls, gaudy synths and vocal samples lifted from happy hardcore, house, hip-hop, R&B and pop hits. Blackout Crew from Bolton took the term mainstream with "Put a Donk on It". Its bass stab is one of the roots of 2020s hard-bounce, and Russian hardbass is often described as heavier donk.
genres.name: Donk

genres.definition: Doom metal is the slow branch of metal: sustained, heavily distorted minor-key riffs at 60–90 BPM, a widely spaced backbeat and a clean, mournful sung vocal, taken from Black Sabbath's first albums and kept alive by Pentagram, Saint Vitus, Trouble, Witchfinder General and Candlemass. This note covers traditional and epic doom; its heavier offshoots have their own notes — stoner-doom (fuzz, groove), funeral-doom (slower, growled), drone-metal (no pulse) and sludge-metal (hardcore vocals) — while death-doom (Paradise Lost, My Dying Bride, Anathema) sits between this note, death-metal and gothic-metal.
genres.name: Doom Metal

genres.definition: Doomcore is slow, dark hardcore: a heavily distorted gabber-type kick on every beat at roughly 120–150 BPM (range uncertain), under sustained minor pads, strings and ominous motifs with long reverb and a slow, fade-driven structure. It comes from the Frankfurt PCP circle around Marc Acardipane (The Mover) in the early 1990s and was revived by a small Dutch and German scene in the 2000s. A hardcore kick at well under hardcore tempo with a tonal minor pad is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Doomcore

genres.definition: Downtempo is the beat-based middle of ambient-downtempo: slowed sampled breaks and soft programmed drums at roughly 80–100 BPM under jazz, soul and dub-derived harmony, instrumental or with sparse vocals. It grew out of 1990s London (Mo' Wax, Ninja Tune), Bristol and Vienna (Kruder & Dorfmeister) and became the default "chill" listening style of the 2000s. Trip-hop is its darker, song-based sibling; chillout its cleaner, programmed one.
genres.name: Downtempo

genres.definition: Dream pop is the atmospheric end of indie-pop: breathy vocals and clean, effects-laden guitars sunk in reverb, echo, tremolo and chorus, with texture and mood placed ahead of riffs and lyrics. It formed in the 1980s UK and US around 4AD (Cocteau Twins, This Mortal Coil) and A.R. Kane, who are credited with the term, ran through Galaxie 500, Mazzy Star and Julee Cruise, and was revived in the 2000s–2010s by Beach House and others. It overlaps heavily with shoegaze, of which it is the quieter, cleaner side.
genres.name: Dream Pop

genres.definition: Dream trance is the Italian piano-led trance of 1995–1997: roughly 132–138 BPM, a soft clean kick, a simple bass, string pads and a piano melody that carries the whole track, with short reverb-washed breakdowns and no aggressive drop. Robert Miles' "Children" (DBX, 1995) defined it, a wave of Italian and French producers followed through 1996, and the German "Dream Dance" compilation series carried the name. It is the gentle, melancholic ancestor of the uplifting breakdown.
genres.name: Dream Trance

genres.definition: Drill is the Chicago-born form of trap that emerged in 2011–2012: a half-time 808 grid at 135–145 notated, dark and sparse minor-key motifs, and a deadpan delivery carrying first-person violence and street-conflict lyrics. Chief Keef, Lil Durk, King Louie and producer Young Chop defined it on the South Side; it spread to London (as UK drill, with its own drum grammar) and back to Brooklyn, where a UK-influenced New York drill scene formed in 2017–2020. It is trap stripped to menace.
genres.name: Drill

genres.definition: Drone is the sustained-tone branch of ambient: a single pitch, interval or cluster held for the length of the piece, with change limited to timbre, beating partials and slow dynamics. It descends from La Monte Young's 1960s Theatre of Eternal Music and from Indian raga practice, runs through Éliane Radigue and Phill Niblock, and in the 1990s–2020s becomes an electronic and organ-based genre on labels such as Kranky and Touch. Harmony does not move; attention moves within the sound.
genres.name: Drone

genres.definition: Drum and bass is fast breakbeat electronic music at 160–180 BPM in which chopped sampled breaks or programmed two-step drums run over a sub bass that moves at half the drum tempo. It grew out of UK breakbeat hardcore and jungle in 1992–1995 and has since split into liquid, neurofunk, jump-up, techstep, jungle revival and dancefloor strands. The defining tension is the double-time drums against the half-time bass.
genres.name: Drum and Bass

genres.definition: Drumfunk is the drum-led strand of drum-and-bass in which breaks sampled from live funk and jazz drumming are chopped hit by hit and re-sequenced into patterns that change every bar, with an understated sub and sparse chords mixed under the drums. It continues the 1990s "choppage" of Paradox, Photek and Source Direct and took its name in the 2000s around Inperspective and Paradox Music. Constant drum variation at drum-and-bass tempo is the identifier.
genres.name: Drumfunk

genres.definition: Dub is the remix practice of reggae turned into a genre: a studio engineer strips a recorded song down to its drums and bass, drops other parts in and out, and throws tape delay, spring reverb and filter sweeps across the remaining fragments. It emerged in Kingston studios around 1972–1974 (dating uncertain) as the instrumental "version" on the B-side and became a standalone form. Its mixing-desk techniques spread to dub-techno, dubstep, trip-hop and post-punk.
genres.name: Dub

genres.definition: Dub techno applies the mixing-desk techniques of Jamaican dub (feedback delay, spring reverb, dropouts, tape saturation) to a slow four-on-the-floor techno pulse. It was defined by Basic Channel (Moritz von Oswald and Mark Ernestus) and the Chain Reaction label in Berlin from 1993. Tracks are long, quiet, harmonically static and textural: one or two chords echoing over a soft kick and a bed of hiss.
genres.name: Dub Techno

genres.definition: Dubstep is half-time electronic bass music notated at 138–142 BPM: a kick on 1, a single snare on 3, and a sustained or LFO-modulated sub bass that carries the track. It formed in South London around 2002–2005 from the darker end of UK garage, grime and dub sound-system culture, then split into the sparse UK original and the mid-range-heavy US "brostep" of 2010–2014. The sub bass, not the drums, is the lead instrument.
genres.name: Dubstep

genres.definition: Dungeon synth is the melodic, lo-fi cousin of dark-ambient: slow minor-key melodies on cheap synth presets (choir, harpsichord, flute, strings) with hall reverb and tape hiss, themed on dungeons, castles and fantasy. It began in the early-1990s Norwegian black-metal circle as "dark dungeon music" (Mortiis, Burzum's keyboard work) and was revived as a Bandcamp genre in the 2010s. Unlike dark ambient it has tunes and phrases; unlike new age it is lo-fi and gloomy.
genres.name: Dungeon Synth

genres.definition: Dutch house is the Netherlands' 2008–2011 variant of electro-house: 128–130 BPM, a punchy kick, a high-pitched, clean lead with pitch-bend slides as the hook, and tribal or Latin percussion fills, with vocal shouts and little harmony. Chuckie's "Dirty Dutch" parties gave it its alias; Afrojack, Sidney Samson, Laidback Luke and early Hardwell carried it into the US EDM boom, where it hardened into big room. Slowed to 108 BPM it became moombahton.
genres.name: Dutch House

genres.definition: Early hardcore is the first wave of hardcore (roughly 1990–1998) as a period and retro category: 160–190 BPM, a thin, clipped analogue 909 kick without sub layer, hoover and rave stabs, sampled speech and a loop-based form, produced on samplers and mastered loud but not brickwalled. The Dutch scene uses "early" for its own 1990s gabber catalogue; this note takes the wider view and also covers the Frankfurt PCP, Belgian, Italian and New York strands. The thin clipped kick with no sub and the rave-era stab palette separate it from everything produced after 2000.
genres.name: Early Hardcore

genres.definition: East Coast hip-hop is the New York-centred regional strand of hip-hop, defined from the late 1980s by sample-based production, chopped break drums and a lyric-first aesthetic that prizes dense rhyme schemes and verse writing over hooks. It contains boom bap as its core drum grammar, but also the glossy, R&B-hooked commercial sound of late-1990s New York and the sparse, cold loops of mid-1990s Queens and Staten Island. The label became meaningful in opposition to the West Coast in the early 1990s.
genres.name: East Coast Hip-Hop

genres.definition: EBM (electronic body music) is the dance form of industrial music from early-1980s Belgium and West Germany: a sequenced, repetitive analog bass line, drum machines, shouted or deadpan command-like vocals and sampled machine sounds, built for the body rather than the head. DAF, Die Krupps, Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb define it. It feeds Belgian new-beat, Birmingham and Berlin techno and, through a 2010s–2020s revival, the EBM-tinged side of dark-techno and dark-disco.
genres.name: EBM

genres.definition: EDM and big room is the 2010s festival mainstage strand of electronic dance music: four-on-the-floor at 126–130 BPM, a pop-vocal breakdown, a snare-roll build and a drop that is little more than a kick and a pitched lead in unison. It grew out of Dutch and Swedish electro house and progressive house around 2010–2012 and became the sound of Tomorrowland, Ultra and Las Vegas. "EDM" here means this specific style, not the whole family.
genres.name: EDM & Big Room

genres.definition: Electric blues is blues played on amplified instruments by a band: electric guitar, often amplified harmonica or horns, piano, bass and drum kit, over 12-bar and 8-bar cycles with a shuffle feel. It starts with T-Bone Walker's amplified guitar around 1940 and becomes the dominant form after 1945 in Chicago, Memphis, Houston, Los Angeles and Detroit. Here it is the umbrella for the guitar-led regional strands texas-blues and west-coast-blues; the harmonica-led chicago-blues sits beside it as its own node, and british-blues and contemporary-blues are its later derivatives.
genres.name: Electric Blues

genres.definition: Electro is electronic dance music built on the Roland TR-808 played in broken, syncopated kick-and-snare patterns, with cold synth bass, vocoded vocals and a machine aesthetic. It formed in New York and Detroit in 1982–1985 from Kraftwerk, funk and early hip-hop, fed directly into Detroit techno and Miami bass, and was revived in the 1990s and 2000s by Detroit, Dutch and German producers. Its drum grammar is the opposite of techno: no kick on every beat.
genres.name: Electro

genres.definition: Electro house is the mid-2000s hardening of house that became the base of edm-big-room: four-on-the-floor at 126–130 BPM, a big compressed kick, and a distorted, resonant sawtooth bass-lead riff with heavy sidechain pumping as the hook, with chopped vocals and a breakdown-drop arc. Benny Benassi's "Satisfaction" (2002) is the prototype; Deadmau5, Wolfgang Gartner, the Ed Banger circle and the Dutch school carried it to 2011, when big room and progressive EDM took over the mainstage. The name borrows "electro" for its synth grit, not for electro's broken drums.
genres.name: Electro House

genres.definition: Electro swing is dance music that puts 1920s–1940s swing and hot-jazz material (brass, clarinet, scat, swung ride patterns), sampled or re-recorded, over programmed house, hip-hop or breakbeat drums with a sub bass and sidechain pumping. It coalesced in Vienna and Paris in the mid-2000s (Parov Stelar's "Rough Cuts", 2004; Caravan Palace, 2008) and peaked in the 2010s through compilations (Wagram's "Electro Swing", Freshly Squeezed's "White Mink"), festivals and swing-dance scenes. It is filed under house because the four-on-the-floor variant dominates DJ use, but a large share of the catalogue rides hip-hop and breakbeat patterns instead; the tempo window and the kick field reflect that spread.
genres.name: Electro Swing

genres.definition: Electroclash is the late-1990s and early-2000s revival strand under electro: 1980s electro, synth-pop and Italo pastiche played at 120–130 BPM on cheap analogue machines, with deadpan spoken or half-sung vocals, lo-fi production and an ironic fashion-world attitude. The name was coined by Larry Tee for his 2001 New York festival; the sound came from Munich and Berlin (DJ Hell's International Deejay Gigolo), Detroit (Ersatz Audio) and New York. By 2004 most of the acts it described had dropped the term.
genres.name: Electroclash

genres.definition: Electronic is the family of production-first music made for DJs and sound systems: tracks built from drum machines, samplers and synthesisers (today DAWs), arranged as repeating phrases for mixing rather than as songs. It spans beatless ambient to 200+ BPM hardcore; what unites it is that the recording itself is the instrument, the arrangement is phrase-based (8/16/32 bars) and vocals are optional. This atlas splits the family into 13 sub-families, each a hub for its own tree.
genres.name: Electronic

genres.definition: Electropop is synth-pop with a hard electronic edge: buzzy or distorted synth bass and lead riffs, punchy programmed drums, heavily processed vocals and a loud master, in verse/chorus pop form. The word was used in the early 1980s for the harder synth-pop of Yellow Magic Orchestra, Gary Numan and Soft Cell and returned in the late 2000s for the DAW-era wave of Lady Gaga, Robyn, La Roux and Little Boots, which is the sound this note centres on. Where synth-pop is cool and analogue, electropop is bright, compressed and club-adjacent.
genres.name: Electropop

genres.definition: Euphoric hardstyle is the melodic, major-leaning strand of hardstyle: 150 BPM, a pitched hardstyle kick with moderate distortion, and a drop built around a supersaw lead melody with chord changes and a sung or pitched vocal hook. It became the dominant hardstyle sound around 2008–2012 and is the form that crossed into festival mainstages and pop collaborations. Melody carries the track; the kick supports it.
genres.name: Euphoric Hardstyle

genres.definition: Euro disco is the continental European form of disco, 1976–1983: four-on-the-floor with an offbeat open hat, a sequencer or straight 1/8 octave bass, lavish strings and multi-voice sung choruses in accented English, produced in Munich, Frankfurt and Paris by studio teams rather than bands. Giorgio Moroder's Munich sound and Frank Farian's Boney M. are the poles. It is the parent of Italo disco, Hi-NRG and space disco and the template for 1990s Eurodance.
genres.name: Euro Disco

genres.definition: Euro trance is the chart-pop form of trance from roughly 1998 to 2004: 136–142 BPM, a sung pop chorus placed on top of the drop, a simple saw lead doubling the vocal melody and a 3–4-minute verse-chorus form with short breakdowns. It grew where eurodance producers adopted uplifting-trance leads and bass (Alice Deejay, ATB, Darude, Ian Van Dahl, Lasgo, Kate Ryan) and after 2005 evolved into hands-up. Where vocal trance hides the verse in a long breakdown, euro trance sings through the loudest bar.
genres.name: Euro Trance

genres.definition: Eurodance is the 1990s European club form of dance-pop: a four-on-the-floor kick at 120–150 BPM, a male rap verse answered by a female sung chorus, and a rave piano or hoover synth riff as the instrumental hook. It formed in the late 1980s out of the German rave and house scenes (Snap!, founded 1989, in Frankfurt), peaked roughly 1992–1995 with 2 Unlimited, Culture Beat, Haddaway and Corona across Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Italy, and faded after 1995–96 into hands-up, trance and europop. Its verse/chorus form keeps it in pop; its tempo and riff keep it in clubs.
genres.name: Eurodance

genres.definition: Europop is the continental-European strand of pop: polished, easy-to-remember songs with a plain lead vocal, lightweight lyrics and a short refrain repeated until it sticks, usually sung in English by non-native speakers. It consolidated in the mid-to-late 1960s, topped charts through the 1980s and 1990s (ABBA as the classic model; Roxette, Ace of Base, Aqua, Alcazar, Cascada later) and remains the house style of the Eurovision Song Contest. The 1990s Scandinavian uptempo variant is often called bubblegum dance.
genres.name: Europop

genres.definition: Experimental groups music whose primary concern is sound, process or concept rather than song, groove or tonal form: musique concrète and tape music, electroacoustic composition, noise, drone, free improvisation, sound art, industrial (as a child), power electronics, harsh noise wall, lowercase and glitch at its most abstract, plus the post-1945 avant-garde when it leaves the score and the concert instrument. Common ground is negative: no reliable pulse, no tonal centre, no standard form. industrial is the main named child; ambient and IDM are filed under electronic when they keep a beat grid or tonal pads.
genres.name: Experimental

genres.definition: Festival trap is the EDM form of trap under edm-big-room: the half-time 808 drum grid, hi-hat rolls and booming sub of Southern rap trap rebuilt as instrumental festival music, notated at 140–150 BPM, with brass and siren leads, rap vocal chops, snare-roll builds and brickwall drops. It emerged in 2011–2012 around TNGHT, Baauer, Flosstradamus and RL Grime, peaked with "Harlem Shake" and "Turn Down for What" in 2013, and hybridised with dubstep, hardstyle and moombahton on mainstages.
genres.name: Festival Trap

genres.definition: Florida breaks is the 1990s Orlando and Tampa form of breakbeat: sampled funk breaks layered over 808 drums and a gliding electro bass at 128–135 BPM, with Miami-bass vocal chops, electro-funk stabs and acid lines borrowed from UK rave, arranged as DJ tools. It grew out of Miami bass and electro and ran parallel to UK nu-skool breaks. An 808 kick with a sliding electro bass under a funk break is the identifier.
genres.name: Florida Breaks

genres.definition: Folk and country form the Anglo-American acoustic song family: narrative lead vocals over acoustic guitar, fiddle, banjo, mandolin, steel and a simple two-beat bass, in diatonic three- and four-chord songs. It spans traditional British, Irish and Appalachian folk, the folk revival and singer-songwriter movement, old-time and bluegrass, honky-tonk, Bakersfield and outlaw country, country pop and Nashville mainstream, alt-country and Americana. Non-Anglophone regional traditions are filed under world-regional; country rock and folk rock sit on the border with rock.
genres.name: Folk & Country

genres.definition: Forest is the organic, groove-led offshoot of darkpsy: roughly 146–152 BPM, a dry kick over a modulated acid-type bass whose filter movement is audible in every bar, wooden percussion, no lead melody and reverb-wet FX that imitate woods, insects and water. It grew out of the Parvati Records circle and the Russian and Swedish dark scene in the late 2000s and takes its name from the forest-party settings it is played in (etymology uncertain). Where darkpsy is dry and digital, forest is damp and earthy.
genres.name: Forest Psytrance

genres.definition: Free jazz is jazz that drops the preset chord changes, fixed tempo and chorus form: horns improvise collectively on jazz instruments with blues cries and extended techniques while bass and drums supply energy and texture instead of walking time. It emerged in the late 1950s with Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor, peaked in 1960s New York (Albert Ayler, late John Coltrane, Archie Shepp, Sun Ra) and in the European free scene from 1966 onward (Peter Brötzmann, Globe Unity, FMP). Tempo and key are not defining properties, so both fields stay null.
genres.name: Free Jazz

genres.definition: Free tekno is the fast, raw, acid-driven techno of the European free-party and teknival sound systems: 160–180 BPM, a distorted kick with a bouncing bass, mental 303 and square-wave riffs, sampled dialogue, hardware-jammed structure and a lo-fi master built for outdoor rigs. Spiral Tribe (UK, 1990) seeded it; France (Heretik), the Czech Republic and Italy made it a scene with its own spelling. Its faster, more melodic descendant is hardtek, its acid-led one acidcore.
genres.name: Free Tekno

genres.definition: Freestyle is the sung, Latin-inflected pop branch of electro: syncopated 808 kick figures and sequenced synth bass under full verse-and-chorus songs, Latin percussion, orchestral hits and melodramatic minor-key melodies. It formed in New York's Puerto Rican and Italian-American neighbourhoods and in Miami in 1983–1985, ruled local dance radio until the early 1990s, and bridges electro and the dance-pop that followed. Shannon's "Let the Music Play" (1983) is the usual starting point.
genres.name: Freestyle

genres.definition: French house is the Paris strand of sample-based house from roughly 1995 to 2001: disco and funk loops run through long filter and phaser sweeps and pumping sidechain compression at 120–126 BPM, with vocoder and talkbox hooks and a dry, compressed mix. Daft Punk, Stardust, Cassius, Bob Sinclar, Alan Braxe, Fred Falke and Étienne de Crécy made it on labels such as Roulé, Crydamoure, Source, Versatile and Yellow. The filter sweep is the signature; where disco-house cuts the loop, French house bends it.
genres.name: French House

genres.definition: Frenchcore is the French-rooted strand of hardcore: 190–210 BPM, a distorted kick whose pitched tail bounces as a bass note on every offbeat eighth, and melodic, often sampled leads with a festive or euphoric register. It grew out of the French free-party tekno scene and Paris hardcore in the 1990s (Micropoint, Radium) and became a festival mainstage sound in the 2010s through Dutch producers (Dr. Peacock, Sefa). The pitched offbeat kick-bass bounce at 200 BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Frenchcore

genres.definition: Full-on is the bright, melodic daytime strand of psytrance: 142–148 BPM, a tight kick followed by three bass notes per beat, a modulated saw or FM lead that carries the drop, and a breakdown-drop arc borrowed from club trance. It took shape in Israel around 2000 (Hommega, BNE) and was the dominant psytrance form of the 2000s. "Morning" full-on is bright and major-leaning; "night" or "twilight" full-on is darker and leads toward darkpsy.
genres.name: Full-On Psytrance

genres.definition: Funky house is the bright, polished, disco-flavoured house of the late 1990s and 2000s, centred on the UK: 125–128 BPM, a punchy kick, short sampled disco and funk fragments, a programmed bass and a sung chorus-length hook, mastered loud. It grew out of disco-house and French filter house when UK labels and compilation brands (Hed Kandi, Defected, Ministry of Sound) turned the sample loop into a pop-friendly club format. The term is British; in the US the same records were sold as disco house or vocal house.
genres.name: Funky House

genres.definition: Future bass is the mid-2010s strand under edm-big-room that puts bright, pumping supersaw chord stabs and pitched vocal chops on a half-time trap drum grid: notated 140–160 BPM with a half-time feel, 808 sub, snare on 3, major-leaning harmony and a build-and-drop form. It came out of Glasgow's Rustie and Hudson Mohawke and Sydney's Flume around 2011–2013, grew through SoundCloud, and reached pop with The Chainsmokers, Marshmello and Illenium by 2016. The drop is a chord progression, not a bass line.
genres.name: Future Bass

genres.definition: Future garage is the atmospheric, listening-oriented strand of uk-garage: the two-step kick and shuffled hats of 2-step at 130–138 BPM, slowed in energy and wrapped in reverb pads, vinyl crackle, a soft sub and pitched vocal fragments. Burial's 2006–2007 records are the template; the name was coined by Whistla before the Future Garage Forum opened in November 2009. It keeps garage's drum grammar and drops its party function.
genres.name: Future Garage

genres.definition: Future house is 2010s house at 124–128 BPM in which a pitched, metallic or formant bass lead plays the melody in the drop over a punchy kick, an offbeat bounce and shuffled hats, with a sung pop hook in the break. Tchami (Paris) used the tag for his 2013 edits and Oliver Heldens' "Gecko" (Spinnin', 2013) made it a chart format; Don Diablo's Hexagon and Heldens' Heldeep ran the Dutch strand through 2014–2018. It sits between the EDM main stage and the deep-house revival, and the chart press often filed it as "deep house".
genres.name: Future House

genres.definition: Future rave is the 2019-onward mainstage style under edm-big-room named and defined by David Guetta and MORTEN: four-on-the-floor at 126–128 BPM, a techno-leaning kick with a rolling offbeat bass, and a drop of saturated, distorted rave-stab and supersaw arpeggios in a dark minor key, with pop vocal verses in the breakdown. It brings peak-time techno's drive and 1990s rave timbres into EDM song form and became the sound of Guetta's Hï Ibiza residency in the 2020s.
genres.name: Future Rave

genres.definition: G-funk is the early-1990s Los Angeles form of west-coast-hip-hop: slow funk grooves at 88–98 BPM built from replayed Parliament-Funkadelic and Zapp material, a deep Moog-style bass, a high whistling portamento synth lead, talkbox and sung hooks, under a relaxed rap. Dr. Dre's "The Chronic" (1992) fixed the template and Death Row carried it to the top of the US charts until about 1996. The name combines "gangsta" and "funk"; the sound is the funk, the lyric is usually the gangsta.
genres.name: G-Funk

genres.definition: G-house is 2010s house at 120–126 BPM that loops sampled gangsta-rap and G-funk vocal phrases as the hook over a deep, clean sub bass, dark minor stabs and a shuffled jackin' or deep house groove. Amine Edge & DANCE (Marseille) shaped it around 2012 and fixed it on their CUFF label (2013); Malaa (Paris, Tchami's Confession, 2015) and Destructo (Los Angeles) took it to US festivals, where it overlapped with bass-house. The rap sample is the identity; the production is restrained, dark house rather than EDM.
genres.name: G-House

genres.definition: Gabber is the Rotterdam strand of hardcore: 160–200+ BPM, an overdriven 909 kick clipped into a square-like waveform with no sub tail, hoover stabs, sirens and shouted or sampled vocals. It formed in 1991–1993 as Rotterdam DJs sped up Frankfurt and Belgian hardcore techno, became a Dutch youth culture by 1995 and survives as "early hardcore" alongside the slower mainstream hardcore it spawned. The word is Amsterdam slang for "mate"; its adoption for the music is usually dated to 1991–1992 (uncertain).
genres.name: Gabber

genres.definition: Gangsta rap is the strand of hip-hop defined by its lyric content: first-person narratives of street crime, gang life, violence and the drug economy, told as reportage, boast or confession. It is a theme, not a production style; it has sat on 808 electro-derived beats, sample loops, G-funk grooves and trap grids. The label was most meaningful from the late 1980s to the late 1990s, when it was the commercial centre of hip-hop and the target of its political backlash.
genres.name: Gangsta Rap

genres.definition: Garage house is the New York and New Jersey strand of house: song-based, gospel-voiced, driven by piano and organ chord riffs and live-feel percussion at 120–126 BPM. The name comes from Larry Levan's Paradise Garage, where the disco-to-house transition played out, and the sound was fixed in New Jersey clubs (Tony Humphries at Zanzibar) and on labels such as Movin', Strictly Rhythm and Nervous. It is the ancestor of UK garage in name and partly in sound, and of soulful house in substance.
genres.name: Garage House

genres.definition: Garage rock is the raw, amateur strand of 1960s rock: teenage bands in the United States and Canada playing fuzz-distorted three-chord songs with a combo organ, shouted vocals and a loud simple backbeat, recorded cheaply, from about 1963 to 1967. It took rock-and-roll, surf-rock and British Invasion beat and R&B covers, stripped them down and played them harder; its 1972 canonisation on the "Nuggets" compilation gave it the first use of "punk rock". Revivals ran in the 1980s and the 2000s.
genres.name: Garage Rock

genres.definition: Ghetto house is the raw 1990s Chicago descendant of chicago-house: a dry 909 or 808 kick at 130–140 BPM, 808 toms and cowbells, a one-note bass and a shouted, repeated, usually explicit chant, with almost no harmony and a lo-fi mix. It was made on the South and West Sides for the Dance Mania label by DJ Deeon, DJ Funk, Paul Johnson, Parris Mitchell, Jammin Gerald and others, and it sped up into juke and footwork at the end of the decade. It is house reduced to kick, chant and attitude.
genres.name: Ghetto House

genres.definition: Ghettotech is Detroit's fast, explicit club offshoot of electro: 145–160 BPM, 808 and 909 drums that switch between four-on-the-floor and electro figures, looped chanted vocals borrowed from Miami bass and Chicago ghetto house, and Detroit techno stabs, all built for fast, scratch-heavy DJ mixing and the jit dance. It formed in the mid-1990s around DJ Assault's and DJ Godfather's labels and has stayed a largely local style.
genres.name: Ghettotech

genres.definition: Glam rock is the British singles-chart rock of 1971–1975: stomping, handclap-doubled backbeats, 1950s rock-and-roll chord cycles played with crunchy guitars, chanted sing-along choruses and a theatrical, androgynous stage image. T. Rex, David Bowie, Slade, Sweet, Mott the Hoople, Roxy Music, Gary Glitter and Suzi Quatro define the UK strand; the New York Dolls, Alice Cooper and Kiss the US one. Its sound fed punk, power-pop and glam-metal; its look outlived its music.
genres.name: Glam Rock

genres.definition: Glitch is the strand of idm whose material is digital failure: CD skips, clicks, buffer stutters, aliasing, dropouts and silence, arranged as rhythm and texture. Oval's "Systemisch" (1994, built from damaged CDs) is the landmark; Mille Plateaux's "Clicks & Cuts" series (2000–), Raster-Noton, Mego and Kim Cascone's "post-digital" essay (2000) codified it. It is colder and sparser than IDM, often without melody, and overlaps with microsound and sound art.
genres.name: Glitch

genres.definition: Glitch hop is broken-beat electronic music at 100–115 BPM that puts programmed hip-hop drums, stutter and buffer-repeat edits, bit-crushed textures and a sidechained, modulated synth bass into a dancefloor arrangement. It has two linked waves: an early-2000s IDM-adjacent form (Prefuse 73, edIT) and a late-2000s to 2010s US and UK bass-music form (The Glitch Mob, KOAN Sound, Opiuo) that DJ charts filed under breakbeat. Micro-edit grammar plus a modulated bass at hip-hop tempo are the identifiers.
genres.name: Glitch Hop

genres.definition: Goa trance is the psychedelic strand of 1990s trance: roughly 138–146 BPM, a moving 1/16 bass line and several interlocking arpeggios and lead lines in eastern-sounding modes, stacked into long, layered tracks. It formed around the beach-party scene of Goa, India, and was produced mainly in the UK, Germany and Israel from about 1992. Around 1997 the sound stripped down and darkened into psytrance, which is now the live umbrella; "goa" names the melodic, layered 1990s form and its revival.
genres.name: Goa Trance

genres.definition: Gqom is the Durban strand of South African house: a raw, minimal, dark sound at 122–128 BPM in which a booming, broken kick pattern is the pulse, harmony is reduced to a drone or a single stab, and chant samples and sirens fill the gaps. It was made by teenagers in the KwaZulu-Natal townships from around 2010–2012 on FL Studio, spread through taxis and phones, and reached Europe through the Gqom Oh! compilation (2016) and DJ Lag. The name is an isiZulu onomatopoeia for a drum hit; it is the only house strand whose kick is not four-on-the-floor.
genres.name: Gqom

genres.definition: Grime is the MC-led offshoot of uk-garage at around 140 BPM: cold, sparse instrumentals of square-wave bass, syncopated or half-time drums and video-game or orchestral stabs, built in 8-bar switches for an MC to rap over. It formed in East London in 2002–2003 from the dark instrumental end of 2-step, with jungle's energy, dancehall's MC culture and hip-hop's verse form. The vocal is the lead instrument; the beat is a frame for it.
genres.name: Grime

genres.definition: Gypsy jazz (jazz manouche) is the string-band swing created in 1930s Paris by Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli's Quintette du Hot Club de France: acoustic lead guitar and violin over two rhythm guitars and bass, with no drums and no horns. It is a branch of jazz that adapts the swing feel to Romani and French musette instrumentation and repertoire, and it has survived as a self-contained scene with its own festivals, luthiers and canon of tunes.
genres.name: Gypsy Jazz

genres.definition: Halftime is drum-and-bass with the two-step drums removed: at the same notated 168–174 BPM the kick lands on 1 and a single snare on 3, so the drums feel like 84–87 BPM hip-hop while the bass design, phrase lengths and sub pressure remain those of drum and bass. It emerged in the UK in the early 2010s from the Autonomic circle, Om Unit and Ivy Lab, with trap, footwork and dubstep as the outside references. One snare per bar at drum-and-bass tempo over neurofunk-grade bass is the identifier.
genres.name: Halftime

genres.definition: Hands up is the commercial, vocal-led edge of hard-dance: 140–150 BPM, a clean punchy kick, a hard offbeat bass on every offbeat eighth, a full sung pop vocal and a supersaw drop that replays the chorus melody. It formed in Germany and the Netherlands around 2002–2005 out of euro-trance, eurodance and italo-dance, peaked in the mid- to late 2000s with chart acts like Cascada and faded after 2010. A full pop song on a hard offbeat bass at 140+ BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Hands Up

genres.definition: Happy hardcore is the major-key, vocal strand of hardcore: 165–175 BPM, a four-on-the-floor kick, a bouncy offbeat bass, piano riffs and sung or pitched-up vocal hooks. It formed in 1993–1995 on two fronts: in the UK out of breakbeat hardcore (keeping a break layer under the kick) and in the Netherlands as "happy gabber" out of Rotterdam gabber, and it crossed into the charts in 1995–1997 before collapsing. Major key plus piano plus a sung hook at 165+ BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Happy Hardcore

genres.definition: Hard bop is the mid-1950s to mid-1960s extension of bebop that pulled the music back toward blues, gospel and rhythm and blues: medium tempos, original compositions with riff and gospel material, a heavier and more interactive drum style and the tenor-and-trumpet quintet as the standard unit. Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, Horace Silver, Clifford Brown and Max Roach, Miles Davis's first quintet, Sonny Rollins, Lee Morgan and Cannonball Adderley are the core; Blue Note, Prestige and Riverside are the labels.
genres.name: Hard Bop

genres.definition: Hard bounce is 2020s hard-techno whose low end bounces: a distorted techno kick on every beat with a tuned bass stab on every offbeat, the device of Spanish makina, UK donk, Russian hardbass and Scottish bouncy-techno, played at 148–160 BPM with trance stabs and a modern loud master. It grew out of German, Spanish, Dutch, UK and Australian hard-techno rooms; in Germany it is tied to the GOTEC club in Karlsruhe and Adrián Mills' 240KM/H label and events, and to a dense layer of SoundCloud labels that describe themselves as "trance, bounce". Event flyers list it beside hard techno and hard trance as its own floor.
genres.name: Hard Bounce

genres.definition: Hard dance is the umbrella for fast, four-on-the-floor electronic styles between trance and hardcore whose kick is distorted and often pitched: hardstyle, hard trance, UK hard house, jumpstyle and their offshoots. It runs 140–165 BPM, pairs an aggressive kick-and-bass layer with euphoric melodies and vocal hooks, and lives on the Dutch and UK festival circuit. The pitched, melody-following kick tail is the trait that unites the umbrella and separates it from techno and hardcore.
genres.name: Hard Dance

genres.definition: Hard house is the UK strand of hard-dance: 145–150 BPM, a hard compressed kick, a bouncy bass stab on every offbeat eighth, hoover riffs and camp or shouted vocal samples, with short breakdowns and a loop-driven structure. It grew out of London's gay club scene (Trade, Tony De Vit) in the mid-1990s from hi-nrg and acid-house, peaked around 1999–2003 on Tidy Trax and Nukleuz and fed the UK side of hard trance and hardstyle. The offbeat bass stab under a non-pitched kick is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Hard House
