genres.definition: Hard NRG is the faster, darker offshoot of UK hard-house: 150–160 BPM, a heavier distorted kick, a hard offbeat bass stab and screeching riffs with hard trance style builds and almost no camp vocal samples. It formed in the London hard dance scene around 1999–2002 (dating uncertain) and sits between hard house, hard trance and early hardstyle. It is thinly documented; tempo and era here are beliefs, not sourced facts.
genres.name: Hard NRG

genres.definition: Hard rock is the loud, riff-driven mainstream of rock: distorted guitar riffs on blues-pentatonic shapes, a heavy backbeat, extended guitar solos and a high tenor vocal, in verse/chorus songs of 4–6 minutes. It grew out of British blues-rock and psychedelic-rock in 1968–1970 (Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple, The Who, Free), ran through AC/DC, Aerosmith, Van Halen and Guns N' Roses, and borders heavy-metal (more gain, more speed), glam-rock (more stomp, less solo), arena-rock (more polish, more keys), grunge (fuzz, loud-quiet) and stoner-rock (down-tuned fuzz grooves).
genres.name: Hard Rock

genres.definition: Hard techno is the fast, distorted end of techno: four-on-the-floor between 140 and 175 BPM, a kick that is the loudest element and carries a rumble tail, aggressive and functional. The term covers two linked waves: the 1990s–2000s Frankfurt and Rotterdam loop-techno lineage that produced schranz, and the 2020s revival built on rumble kicks, 150+ BPM and borrowed hardstyle and trance gestures. Melody is subordinate to kick, bass pressure and hat density.
genres.name: Hard Techno

genres.definition: Hard trance is the harder, faster end of trance filed under hard-dance: 140–150 BPM, a compressed, lightly saturated kick, a separate offbeat or rolling bass line, acid lines and minor-key saw riffs over a trance breakdown-build-drop arc. It formed in Germany and the Netherlands in the mid-1990s, peaked around 1998–2003 and supplied hardstyle with its leads and arrangement. A hard kick without a pitched tail plus a trance bass line is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Hard Trance

genres.definition: Hardbass is Russian hard dance from late-1990s Saint Petersburg: 150–175 BPM, a heavy distorted kick, punchy offbeat "donk" basslines, distorted stabs and occasional chanted or rapped vocals, in minimal, repetitive loops. It became an internet meme around 2010 through satirical videos and masked public dance flash mobs. Its offbeat bass ties it to UK donk and makes it one of the roots of 2020s hard-bounce.
genres.name: Hardbass

genres.definition: Hardcore is the fastest and most distorted four-on-the-floor branch of electronic dance music: 160 BPM and above, a clipped, square-like kick that dominates the mix, hoover stabs and MC or sampled vocals. It formed in 1990–1992 out of Frankfurt and Belgian hard techno, Rotterdam's gabber scene and the UK breakbeat rave, and it now covers gabber, mainstream hardcore, happy hardcore, frenchcore, uptempo, industrial hardcore and terror/speedcore. The clipped kick with no sub tail is the trait that unites the umbrella.
genres.name: Hardcore

genres.definition: Hardcore hip-hop is the aggressive register of hip-hop: shouted or forceful delivery, confrontational content and hard, loud drums, with either a dense noise-collage or a stark minimal loop underneath. It formed in New York in the mid-1980s with Run-DMC, Schoolly D and Public Enemy, became the dominant mode of 1990s New York rap (Wu-Tang Clan, Onyx, Mobb Deep, M.O.P.) and gave horrorcore its root. It is defined by intensity, not by region or by a single drum grammar.
genres.name: Hardcore Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Hardgroove is percussive, swung, loop-based techno at 140–150 BPM: a heavy but clean kick under syncopated conga and tom loops, chopped vocal shouts and funky stabs. The name comes from Ben Sims' Hardgroove label (London, 1999), which fixed the sound in the 2000s, and it returned as a scene term in the 2020s revival (Alarico, Chlär and Funk Assault, Bastet and others) as the groovy counterweight to hard-techno. It is the faster, kick-heavier descendant of tribal-techno.
genres.name: Hardgroove

genres.definition: Hardstep is the 1995–1997 London strand of drum-and-bass that stripped jungle down to a hard two-step kick and snare from a single break, a heavy sub bass and sparse dark stabs, with hip-hop samples instead of ragga toasting. It is the transitional form between jungle and both techstep and jump-up. Low snare density over a sampled break, a bass that stays below 150 Hz and a dark, stripped palette are the identifiers.
genres.name: Hardstep

genres.definition: Hardstyle is the Dutch core of hard-dance: 150–155 BPM, a distorted kick whose tonal tail follows the bass note, a reverse bass in the intro and a euphoric melodic breakdown. It formed in 1999–2002 as Dutch and Italian producers slowed hardcore and hardened trance, grew into the Q-dance festival circuit in the 2000s and split into euphoric and raw strands in the 2010s. The pitched kick tail is the single defining trait.
genres.name: Hardstyle

genres.definition: Hardtek is the faster, melodic, hook-driven form of free-tekno that French free-party producers developed in the 2000s: 175–195 BPM, a distorted kick with an offbeat bass bounce, anthemic synth or sampled-vocal hooks and breakbeat interludes, mastered brighter than classic tekno. It is the strand of tekno that crossed into clubs and festivals and sits next to frenchcore without adopting the hardcore kick. raggatek is its ragga-sampling child.
genres.name: Hardtek

genres.definition: Heavy metal in the narrow sense is the traditional form of metal: mid-tempo riff songs with two distorted guitars, harmonised twin leads, a clean high tenor vocal, galloping rhythms and extended solos, as codified by Judas Priest, Iron Maiden and the New Wave of British Heavy Metal around 1978–1983. It sits between hard-rock and the extreme branches that split from it: faster (speed-metal, thrash-metal, power-metal), slower (doom-metal), more polished (glam-metal) or longer-form (progressive-metal). Melody, both vocal and guitar, stays in front.
genres.name: Heavy Metal

genres.definition: Hi-NRG is the fast, synthesiser-driven form of disco that grew in gay clubs in San Francisco, New York and London from 1977 onward: 126–136 BPM, a kick on every beat, an octave synth bass on every eighth without rest, loud claps and belted camp vocals. Patrick Cowley, Bobby Orlando and Ian Levine are its producers; Stock Aitken Waterman took it to the UK pop charts in 1984–1986. It feeds UK hard house, Eurobeat and 1990s handbag house.
genres.name: Hi-NRG

genres.definition: Hi-tech is the fastest offshoot of darkpsy: roughly 165–185 BPM, a clicky kick over a fast 1/16 rolling psy bass, and a bright, dry layer of glitch edits, stutters, pitch-shifted vocal snippets and digital zaps in place of melody. It formed around 2008–2012 among Russian, German and later Portuguese and South American producers (Kindzadza, Highko, Psykovsky) and sits where psytrance borders hardcore tempos. Where darkpsy is menacing, hi-tech is manic and cartoonish.
genres.name: Hi-Tech Psytrance

genres.definition: Hill country blues is the country-blues of the North Mississippi hill country east of the Delta (Marshall, Panola and Tate counties around Holly Springs, Como and Senatobia): a droning, riff-based style that stays on one or two chords, drives a steady groove and treats the 12-bar form as optional. Mississippi Fred McDowell, R. L. Burnside, Junior Kimbrough, Jessie Mae Hemphill and the fife-and-drum bands of Othar Turner and Napoleon Strickland are its core; Fat Possum Records' 1990s releases made it a recognised style and a model for the garage-blues of the 2000s.
genres.name: Hill Country Blues

genres.definition: Hip-hop is music built around a rapped lead vocal over a looped beat. The beat is sampled or programmed, the drums carry a backbeat rather than a four-on-the-floor kick, and the rap is the primary element for most of the duration. The family spans boom bap, gangsta rap, Southern and trap production, drill, conscious and alternative rap, UK rap and a large pop-rap overlap.
genres.name: Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Hip house is house with full rapped verses: a Chicago-style 120–126 BPM groove of 909 kick, clap, piano stabs and synth bass under an MC's party rap and a sung or shouted chorus. It started in Chicago in 1987–1988 (Tyree Cooper, Fast Eddie, Kool Rock Steady on DJ International) and New York (Jungle Brothers' "I'll House You"), and peaked in the charts in 1989–1991 with Technotronic, Doug Lazy and the UK and Belgian pop variants. It is the ancestor of South African kwaito and, at a distance, of 2010s g-house.
genres.name: Hip House

genres.definition: Horrorcore is the strand of hardcore-hip-hop that borrows its imagery from horror film and the occult: slasher narratives, demons, psychosis and gore, delivered over beats that sample or imitate horror scores. It is defined by content and palette, not by a drum grammar; it has sat on New York boom bap, Memphis tape production and later trap. Its roots are split between Houston (Geto Boys), Detroit (Esham) and Memphis (Three 6 Mafia), with a New York peak in 1994.
genres.name: Horrorcore

genres.definition: House is four-on-the-floor electronic dance music at 115–135 BPM built from drum-machine grooves, disco and soul samples, chord stabs and sung vocal hooks. It formed in Chicago and New York clubs in the mid-1980s as DJs and producers rebuilt disco with 808s, 909s and samplers. The kick is steady but warm; the groove comes from swung hats, bass line and chords rather than from kick pressure.
genres.name: House

genres.definition: Hyperpop is pop exaggerated to breaking point: pitch-shifted and heavily Auto-Tuned vocals, clipped and distorted masters, brash synth melodies, metallic percussion, catchy choruses and very short songs with abrupt edits. It grew out of the London label PC Music (founded 2013; A. G. Cook, SOPHIE, Hannah Diamond, GFOTY) and Charli XCX's work with them, was popularised by 100 gecs in 2019 and named by Spotify's "hyperpop" playlist (August 2019, the tag having entered its metadata in 2018), then spread through SoundCloud (glaive, ericdoa, osquinn, underscores). Maximalism and deliberate artificiality are the signature.
genres.name: Hyperpop

genres.definition: Hypertechno is internet-native, song-length hard-techno: a familiar pop, eurodance or 2000s dance vocal hook, sped up and pitched up, over a distorted techno kick at 150–165 BPM, built for TikTok clips, streaming playlists and phone speakers. It grew in German-speaking countries in the early 2020s together with the sped-up-song trend and the move of hard techno to festival main stages. No reliable source codifies it; the term is a playlist and platform label, and its line to German tekk bootlegs is blurred.
genres.name: Hypertechno

genres.definition: Hyphy is the mid-2000s San Francisco Bay Area strand of west-coast-hip-hop: sparse, bass-and-clap beats with staccato synth bass, siren and whistle stabs and chanted dance hooks, under a fast, loose, slang-heavy delivery. It grew out of Bay Area mobb music and the local car and sideshow culture and peaked nationally around 2005–2007. The word means hyperactive; the music is built for dancing and shouting, not for listening to verses.
genres.name: Hyphy

genres.definition: Hypnotic techno is techno built for trance states rather than peaks: dense, layered, polyrhythmic percussion and slowly evolving drones over a steady 130–136 BPM kick, with no melody, no vocals and no drops. It grew out of minimal-techno and dub-techno in the late 2000s, with Donato Dozzy, Prologue (Munich), Semantica (Madrid) and the Italian school as its centre, and Beatport's "Raw / Deep / Hypnotic" category (2020) gave it a market name.
genres.name: Hypnotic Techno

genres.definition: IDM is home-listening electronic music built on complex, constantly changing programmed drums and melodic synth writing, filed under ambient-downtempo because it is made for the armchair rather than the floor. The name comes from a 1993 mailing list discussing Warp's "Artificial Intelligence" compilation (1992); Aphex Twin, Autechre, The Black Dog, B12, Squarepusher and Boards of Canada are its canon, Rephlex's "braindance" its rival name. Tempo is not a defining property; drum complexity and melody are.
genres.name: IDM

genres.definition: Indie pop is the independent-label strand of pop: melodic, guitar-based songs with jangly clean guitars, a dry and understated lead vocal, a live kit and DIY production values, deliberately less abrasive than indie rock and less polished than the charts. It grew out of late-1970s UK post-punk (Postcard Records, 1979; Orange Juice), was codified by NME's *C86* compilation (1986) and Sarah Records, and has run through Belle and Sebastian, Camera Obscura, The Pains of Being Pure at Heart and later waves. Twee pop is its most self-consciously gentle subset.
genres.name: Indie Pop

genres.definition: Industrial is the experimental music of noise, metal percussion, tape manipulation and harsh or processed vocals that formed around Throbbing Gristle and Industrial Records in 1976–1977 and spread through Cabaret Voltaire, SPK, Einstürzende Neubauten and their peers. It is non-dance music in song or collage form with no steady 4/4 kick; later descendants added beats and became EBM, industrial rock and metal (Ministry, Nine Inch Nails, Rammstein) and, in club music, industrial-techno. This note covers the core and the EBM and rock branches as they keep song form and a non-club kick.
genres.name: Industrial

genres.definition: Industrial hardcore is the noise-led, hook-free strand of hardcore: 160–190 BPM, a distorted dry kick under sustained noise textures, metallic percussion and drones, with no melodic or vocal hook and a loop structure instead of breakdowns and drops. It formed in the Netherlands, Germany and the UK in the late 1990s out of darker gabber, industrial music and industrial-techno, and it supplies the textures that crossbreed and darker mainstream hardcore borrow. Sustained mid-band noise with no hook at hardcore tempo is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Industrial Hardcore

genres.definition: Industrial techno is techno that takes its textures from industrial music: noise, metal percussion, drones, distortion and a cold, hostile atmosphere over a four-on-the-floor kick. It has two anchors: the 1990s Birmingham sound (Surgeon, Regis, Downwards) and the 2010s wave centred on Berlin and the UK (Perc Trax, Ancient Methods, Paula Temple, Mord). Texture leads; hooks and melody are nearly absent.
genres.name: Industrial Techno

genres.definition: Italo dance is the Italian late-1990s to mid-2000s successor of eurodance: four-on-the-floor dance-pop with a vocoded or pitch-corrected sung vocal, a piano or plucked synth lead melody as the hook and a "metallic" sawtooth bassline, with no rapper. It emerged in mid-1990s Italy, peaked from the late 1990s to the mid-2000s — Eiffel 65's "Blue (Da Ba Dee)" reached number one in several countries in 1999 — and is represented by Gigi D'Agostino, Gabry Ponte, Prezioso, Paps'n'Skar and Neja. The instrumental lead melody is the hook; the vocal is a texture around it.
genres.name: Italo Dance

genres.definition: Italo disco is the synthesiser-and-drum-machine form of disco made in Italy in 1982–1988: kick on every beat with a clap and an offbeat open hat, octave synth bass on straight 1/8, Juno and DX7 chords, vocoder touches and sung English choruses with melancholic minor melodies. The name comes from the German label ZYX's compilation series (1983). It links late-1970s Euro disco to Chicago house and is the model for the electroclash, synthwave and nu-disco revivals.
genres.name: Italo Disco

genres.definition: Italo house is the Italian strand of house from roughly 1988 to 1992: a riffing piano in octave chords, sampled diva phrases, bright string pads and a 909 groove at 120–126 BPM, mixed glossy and aimed at the charts. It came out of the Adriatic Riviera clubs and studios around Rimini, Bologna and Brescia and broke internationally with Black Box's "Ride on Time" (1989). The piano riff is the identity; later Italian strands (dream house, Italo dance) kept the melody but left the house groove.
genres.name: Italo House

genres.definition: J-core is Japanese hardcore: the UK hardcore and happy hardcore template (170–190 BPM, offbeat bass, supersaw leads) plus gabber and speedcore kicks, rebuilt with Japanese-language anime, game and vocaloid vocals, chiptune timbres and dense, fast-modulating harmony. It grew in the Tokyo doujin (self-published) scene from the late 1990s (DJ Sharpnel) and spread through Comiket circles and rhythm-game soundtracks in the 2000s and 2010s. Japanese vocal samples and chiptune leads over a hardcore kick are the fingerprint.
genres.name: J-Core

genres.definition: Jackin' house is the bumpy, heavily swung, sample-chopping strand of house: 124–128 BPM, a sidechained kick, shuffled hats, a bouncing bass and disco, funk or soul samples cut into 1–2-beat stutters, mixed loud. The name comes from the Chicago "jack" of the 1980s and the 1990s Cajual and Relief "bumpin'" records of DJ Sneak, Derrick Carter and Paul Johnson, but as a genre tag it belongs to the 2000s and 2010s, when UK producers and Beatport fixed it as a category. It is the rawer, swingier cousin of funky-house and a direct ancestor of UK bass-house.
genres.name: Jackin' House

genres.definition: Jazz is improvisation-centred ensemble music from African-American communities in the early-20th-century United States, built on swing rhythm, blues inflection and European harmony extended into 7ths, 9ths and altered dominants. A rhythm section (bass, drums, piano or guitar) supports horn or keyboard soloists over repeating chord cycles. Branches include New Orleans and Dixieland, swing and big band, bebop, cool, hard bop, modal, free, Latin jazz, fusion, smooth jazz, nu jazz and the 2010s–2020s UK and Los Angeles revival. Tempo and instrumentation vary widely; swing feel and improvisation over changing harmony are the constants.
genres.name: Jazz

genres.definition: Jazz-funk is the danceable end of jazz-fusion: 1970s funk grooves at 95–120 BPM with the kick on the one, a syncopated electric bass riff, Rhodes, clavinet and synthesizers, wah guitar and horn riffs, with jazz solos kept short and the vamp kept long. Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters, Donald Byrd's Mizell-produced Blue Note albums, Roy Ayers, the Crusaders and the CTI/Kudu roster define the American sound; Britain's Brit-funk wave of 1979–83 (Light of the World, Incognito, Level 42's early work) extends it. It is the most sampled and DJ-played branch of jazz.
genres.name: Jazz-Funk

genres.definition: Jazz fusion is jazz improvisation on electric instruments over rock and funk grooves: Rhodes and synthesizers, distorted guitar, electric bass and a drummer playing straight 1/8s and odd meters at rock volume, with long virtuosic solos and through-composed sections. It emerged from Miles Davis's electric bands of 1968–1970 and the groups his sidemen formed (Weather Report, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Return to Forever, Herbie Hancock's bands), ran parallel in Britain (Soft Machine, Nucleus) and remains a live, instrumental virtuoso tradition. The electric timbre and the straight grid are its fingerprints.
genres.name: Jazz Fusion

genres.definition: Jazz rap is the strand of alternative-hip-hop built on jazz: sampled upright bass, horn phrases, Rhodes and piano chords with 7ths and 9ths, and ride-cymbal textures, laid over boom-bap drums at 86–96 BPM under a relaxed, conversational rap. It formed in New York in 1988–1991 with Stetsasonic, Gang Starr and A Tribe Called Quest and peaked in 1991–1994; its loops and mood became the raw material of lo-fi hip-hop two decades later. The jazz is in the samples and the harmony, not usually in improvisation.
genres.name: Jazz Rap

genres.definition: Jersey club is the Newark, New Jersey descendant of baltimore-club: a clustered, triplet-like five-kick figure at 132–140 BPM, the "bed squeak" sample as a rhythmic hook, and vocal chops cut into 1/16 stutters from R&B, pop and rap a cappellas, over programmed 808 claps rather than a sampled break. It formed in the early 2000s around DJ Tameil and the Brick Bandits and reached pop and rap production in 2022–2023. The kick cluster plus the bed squeak plus stuttered chops are the identifiers.
genres.name: Jersey Club

genres.definition: Juke and footwork are the fast Chicago descendants of ghetto-house: 155–165 BPM, 808 kicks and toms in syncopated, triplet-leaning patterns that abandon the four-on-the-floor, an 808 sub, rapid hat rolls and vocal samples chopped into stutters. Juke (late 1990s) kept ghetto house's chants and party function; footwork (2000s) grew around the dance battles of the South and West Sides and became sparser, more abstract and more sample-driven (RP Boo, DJ Rashad, DJ Spinn, Traxman, Teklife). Planet Mu's "Bangs & Works" (2010) and Hyperdub took it worldwide, where its 160 BPM tempo put it beside jungle and drum and bass.
genres.name: Juke / Footwork

genres.definition: Jump blues is up-tempo blues played by a swing-era small combo: a shouted vocal over a horn section riffing on 12-bar cycles, with a boogie-woogie bass, swing drums and honking tenor-sax solos. Louis Jordan's Tympany Five (Decca, from 1938) set the format; Kansas City shouters (Big Joe Turner, Jimmy Rushing), Los Angeles bands (Roy Milton, Amos Milburn, Johnny Otis) and the King and Savoy rosters (Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown, Tiny Bradshaw) filled the 1940s charts. It is the fast end of 1940s rhythm-and-blues and a direct source of rock-and-roll.
genres.name: Jump Blues

genres.definition: Jump-up is the hook-led, party strand of drum-and-bass: loud, simple two-step drums at 172–176 BPM under a mid-range "talking" bass riff that repeats every 1–2 bars with filter, pitch or formant movement, plus MC hype and comedic FX. It formed in London in 1995–1997 out of hardstep and ragga jungle (Ganja Kru, Urban Takeover) and became the dominant club and festival strand of the 2010s and 2020s. The mid-range bass riff as the hook is the identifier.
genres.name: Jump-Up

genres.definition: Jumpstyle is the Belgian and Dutch strand of hard-dance built on a distorted kick on every beat and a pitched bass note on every offbeat eighth that follows a simple melody, at 140–150 BPM, with short pop-derived lead riffs. It grew out of Belgian "jump" (hardcore and gabber slowed down with an offbeat bass) in the late 1990s and peaked in 2007–2009 when the jumpstyle dance went viral and tracks charted in Belgium and the Netherlands. The melody-following offbeat bass under a distorted kick, present through the whole track, is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Jumpstyle

genres.definition: Jungle is the 1992–1995 London form of drum-and-bass built from chopped, pitched-up funk breaks (Amen, Think, Apache) at 160–170 BPM over a reggae-derived sub bass moving at half the drum tempo. It is the point where UK breakbeat hardcore sheds its rave pianos and takes on dancehall bass lines, time-stretched vocals and MC culture. Today the name covers both the 1990s records and a 2010s–2020s revival that reuses the same breaks and sampling grammar.
genres.name: Jungle

genres.definition: Krautrock is the West German experimental rock of roughly 1968–1977: repetitive, trance-inducing pieces built on a metronomic drum pulse (the motorik beat), one- or two-chord vamps, analogue electronics and tape editing, with vocals sparse or absent. Can, Neu!, early Kraftwerk, Faust, Amon Düül II, Cluster, Harmonia and Ash Ra Tempel took psychedelic-rock and stripped the blues out, borrowing from minimalism, free-jazz and electroacoustic music instead. The British press coined the name; the bands preferred "kosmische Musik". Its pulse and stasis fed post-rock, electronic music and the ambient berlin-school.
genres.name: Krautrock

genres.definition: Kwaito is South Africa's township reworking of house from the early 1990s: the house drum pattern slowed to roughly 100–110 BPM, a looped keyboard riff and a deep bass under chanted, rapped and sung vocals in isiZulu, Sesotho, tsotsitaal and English. It emerged in Johannesburg and Soweto as apartheid ended and was the dominant Black South African youth music of the late 1990s and early 2000s (Arthur Mafokate, Boom Shaka, Trompies, TKZee, Mandoza, Zola). Its slow house groove and chant delivery feed directly into gqom and amapiano.
genres.name: Kwaito

genres.definition: Latin groups the popular musics of Latin America, the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, Brazil and Spain: Afro-Cuban son and salsa, merengue, bachata, cumbia, vallenato, mariachi and regional Mexican (norteño, banda, corridos), tango, bossa nova and samba, flamenco and Latin pop, and the reggaeton and Latin trap wave of the 2000s–2020s. Common ground: Spanish or Portuguese vocals, clave-derived rhythmic cells and hand-percussion timbres from the Afro-Caribbean lineage. Tempo and instrumentation differ sharply between branches; language and rhythmic cell are the shared tests.
genres.name: Latin

genres.definition: Latin house is house built with Afro-Cuban and wider Latin American elements: congas in tumbao, timbales, güiro and clave patterns, a piano montuno or brass stabs and Spanish-language hooks over a 124–128 BPM four-on-the-floor. It formed in New York in the early 1990s around Masters at Work and the Nuyorican Soul project, ran through Miami and Chicago, took a Spanish-guitar turn in 2000s Ibiza and returned in the 2020s as a Latin strand of tech house. Rhythm cells from salsa and the Latin percussion set are the identity; the kick is standard house.
genres.name: Latin House

genres.definition: Latin jazz is jazz improvisation over Latin American rhythm sections: Afro-Cuban clave-based percussion with tumbao bass and montuno piano, or Brazilian samba and bossa nova grooves with nylon guitar and light percussion. It began in 1940s New York when Cuban bandleaders and bebop players met (Machito, Mario Bauzá, Dizzy Gillespie with Chano Pozo), gained a Brazilian strand through Stan Getz and the bossa nova wave of the 1960s, and continues through Cuban, Puerto Rican and Brazilian players on both sides of the exchange. Straight 1/8s with a clave or bossa accent cell replace swing; the solo language stays jazz.
genres.name: Latin Jazz

genres.definition: Liquid drum and bass is the melodic, soulful strand of drum-and-bass: clean two-step drums at 170–176 BPM under moving chord progressions, sung vocals or soul, funk and disco samples, and a warm sub bass that follows the harmony. Fabio named it "liquid funk" in 2000; Hospital Records and Calibre made it the largest listening strand of the genre in the 2000s and 2010s. Harmony and vocals as lead elements are the identifiers.
genres.name: Liquid Drum and Bass

genres.definition: Lo-fi house is 2010s house at 118–123 BPM that reproduces a deep or Chicago house palette through deliberate degradation: tape hiss, saturation, bit reduction, muffled highs, pitch wobble and uneven levels. It grew out of the "outsider house" of L.I.E.S. and 1080p and broke through a wave of YouTube uploads in 2016–2017 (DJ Boring, Mall Grab, DJ Seinfeld, Ross From Friends, Lobster Theremin), where the dusty sound and the ironic names were the point. Musically it is deep house; the identity is the production treatment.
genres.name: Lo-Fi House

genres.definition: Loop techno is functional DJ-tool techno of roughly 1996–2006: a clean, punchy kick at 134–142 BPM under two to four interlocking percussion and filtered stab loops, changed by slow filter movement and mutes, with no melody, vocals or drops. Jeff Mills' Purpose Maker series defined it, Sweden's Drumcode and H-Productions, the UK's Primate and Ben Sims circle and Italy's Zenit made it the dominant hard-but-clean techno of the period. hardgroove and schranz grew out of it; peak-time-techno replaced it.
genres.name: Loop Techno

genres.definition: Mainstream hardcore is the post-2000 Dutch and Italian form of gabber and the centre of today's hardcore umbrella: 170–180 BPM, a layered digitally produced kick with a sub layer and long distorted body, screech and hoover hooks, MC vocal hooks and brickwall mastering, arranged with breakdowns and drops. It formed around 1999–2003 as "nu-style" when the collapsed gabber scene slowed down and darkened, and it has been the core sound of Masters of Hardcore and Dominator since. The sub-layered modern kick and the breakdown-drop arc separate it from 1990s early hardcore.
genres.name: Mainstream Hardcore

genres.definition: Makina (Spanish mákina) is fast Spanish rave music from early-1990s Valencia: 160–175 BPM, a punchy four-on-the-floor kick with bouncing offbeat bass stabs, and long, catchy synth or piano riffs drawing on Eurodance and hard trance. It grew out of the Valencian bakalao club sound and later became the staple rave sound of North East England and Scotland. Its offbeat bassline is a direct input into 2020s hard-bounce, where DJs such as Adrián Mills put makina basslines under hard-techno kicks.
genres.name: Makina

genres.definition: Melbourne bounce is the Australian 2012–2015 variant under edm-big-room: 126–130 BPM, a punchy kick, a short bass stab on every eighth-note offbeat (the "bounce") and a high, pitch-bending lead riff inherited from Dutch house, in a sparse drop after a snare-roll build. Will Sparks, Joel Fletcher, Orkestrated, Timmy Trumpet and the Melbourne club circuit built it; TJR's "Ode to Oi" (2012) and Deorro took it to the US. The offbeat bass is the same gesture as UK hard house and donk, 20 BPM slower.
genres.name: Melbourne Bounce

genres.definition: Melodic death metal is death-metal with the melody put back: harmonised twin-guitar leads in a stable minor key, derived from Iron Maiden-era heavy-metal, over down-tuned riffs, double-kick drumming and a harsh but articulate growl. It formed in Gothenburg in 1993–1996 (At the Gates, In Flames, Dark Tranquillity), with Carcass's "Heartwork" as the usual precursor, and spread through Finland (Children of Bodom, Insomnium, Amorphis) and Sweden (Arch Enemy, Soilwork). Its riffs became the raw material of 2000s metalcore.
genres.name: Melodic Death Metal

genres.definition: Melodic dubstep is the harmonic, vocal-led strand of brostep: the 140 BPM half-time drop kept, but filled with sustained supersaw chord progressions borrowed from trance and progressive house, a sung lead vocal and a growl bass that supports rather than dominates. It formed in 2011–2012 (Seven Lions, Adventure Club, Blackmill) and scaled to arenas with Illenium after 2016; "melodic bass" is the later umbrella for it and its future-bass hybrids. The chord progression is the hook; the drop is where it lands.
genres.name: Melodic Dubstep

genres.definition: Melodic techno is slow techno (120–126 BPM) led by minor-key arpeggios, wide pads and emotional chord movement over restrained techno drums, with long cinematic breakdowns. It consolidated in the mid-2010s around Tale Of Us (Afterlife), Innervisions, Diynamic and Stephan Bodzin and became the most commercially successful techno strand of the early 2020s, crossing into pop and festival main stages (Anyma). Beatport files it under "Melodic House & Techno" together with its house-side twin, progressive-house.
genres.name: Melodic Techno

genres.definition: Memphis blues is the blues of Beale Street and the Memphis recording industry in two strands: the 1920s–30s jug-band and hokum ensembles (Memphis Jug Band, Cannon's Jug Stompers, Frank Stokes, Furry Lewis, Memphis Minnie) and the raw amplified blues cut at Sun Records and for RPM and Duke in 1949–55 (B. B. King's first hits, Howlin' Wolf's Memphis sides, Junior Parker, Rosco Gordon, Bobby "Blue" Bland). The city is the staging post between the rural Delta (country-blues) and chicago-blues, and later the home of soul-blues.
genres.name: Memphis Blues

genres.definition: Memphis rap is the 1990s underground form of southern-hip-hop from Memphis, Tennessee: lo-fi cassette production on 808 drums in slow, sparse grids, eerie minor pads and horror samples, triplet flows and chanted hooks, with pitched-down and whispered vocal layers. DJ Spanish Fly, Tommy Wright III, Three 6 Mafia and the Hypnotize Minds circle built it on hand-dubbed tapes; its triplet flow and dark palette became the raw material of crunk, trap and phonk. Its sound is tape hiss, 808 and chant.
genres.name: Memphis Rap

genres.definition: Metal is the high-gain, riff-driven descendant of rock: distorted and often down-tuned guitars, dense drumming with double kick, dark modal harmony, and vocals ranging from operatic to growled. It emerged around 1970 in Britain and branched widely: traditional and NWOBHM, thrash, death, black, doom, power, progressive, groove, metalcore, nu metal, symphonic and djent. Loudness and riff weight define it more than tempo, which spans 60 to 280 BPM.
genres.name: Metal

genres.definition: Miami bass is the Florida branch of electro: syncopated TR-808 drum programming with the kick tuned low and left to ring, rapped and chanted party vocals, and a mix built for car trunks and skating rinks. It formed in Miami around 1985 out of electro-funk and hip-hop, peaked commercially in the mid-1990s with national dance-craze singles, and fed Southern hip-hop, Baltimore club and ghettotech. The 808 sub "boom" is the genre.
genres.name: Miami Bass

genres.definition: Microhouse is house built from tiny sounds: a clean kick at 120–126 BPM under clicks, pops and sub-second samples of funk, radio and vocal shards arranged on a precise grid, with harmony reduced to fragments and a quiet, high-resolution mix. It formed around 1997–2002 in Frankfurt (Playhouse, Perlon), Cologne (Kompakt) and Montreal (Akufen, Mutek), with the Force Inc and Mille Plateaux "Clicks & Cuts" releases as its manifesto, and the name is credited to critic Philip Sherburne (2001, uncertain). It is the house-side twin of minimal-techno and was absorbed by the mid-2000s minimal boom.
genres.name: Microhouse

genres.definition: Minimal techno is techno stripped to its functional core: a clean kick, a handful of percussive and tonal elements, and change achieved by slow modulation rather than new parts. It began with Robert Hood's and Daniel Bell's early-1990s reductionism and Richie Hawtin's Plastikman, and peaked as the mid-2000s "minimal" boom around 125–128 BPM (Berlin, Perlon, Minus, Kompakt), where it blurred into tech-house.
genres.name: Minimal Techno

genres.definition: Modal jazz is jazz improvised over modes or single chords held for long stretches rather than over fast-moving functional chord changes. It took shape around Miles Davis's "Milestones" (1958) and Kind of Blue (1959), George Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept and the John Coltrane quartet (1960–65), and it gave soloists harmonic room, pianists quartal voicings and bassists pedal points. It is less a scene than a harmonic method that later styles (post-bop, spiritual jazz, fusion) absorbed.
genres.name: Modal Jazz

genres.definition: Moombahton is the 108 BPM hybrid under edm-big-room that Dave Nada created in 2009 by slowing a Dutch house record to reggaeton tempo: a kick on every beat with a dembow snare figure, slowed Dutch house leads with pitch slides, reggaeton and dancehall percussion, Spanish vocal samples and an EDM build-and-drop form. Nada, Munchi, Dillon Francis and Diplo's Mad Decent built the scene in 2010–2012; its rhythm fed "Lean On", Justin Bieber's "Sorry" and the 2015–2017 pop-reggaeton wave. It is the only EDM strand here below 120 BPM.
genres.name: Moombahton

genres.definition: Neurofunk is the hi-fi, bass-design-led successor of techstep: 172–176 BPM two-step with clean, precise drums and a bass line built from layered, resampled and modulated patches whose timbre changes on nearly every note, pumped against the kick by sidechain compression. It emerged in London around 1998 with Ed Rush and Optical's Virus Recordings, moved to the Netherlands and central Europe in the 2000s and 2010s, and is now the technical mainstream of dark drum and bass. The moving bass is the hook.
genres.name: Neurofunk

genres.definition: New age is the melodic, consonant relaxation strand of ambient-downtempo: foreground melodies on piano, guitar, harp, flute or voice over major or pentatonic harmony, often with nature sounds, made for meditation, healing and calm listening. It formed in 1970s California (Steven Halpern, Iasos, Windham Hill Records) and peaked commercially in the 1980s (Kitarō, Enya, the Grammy category from 1987). It is defined by function and mood as much as by sound, and can be acoustic, electronic or both.
genres.name: New Age

genres.definition: New beat is the slow, dark Belgian club sound of 1987–1989: EBM, industrial and acid-house records played at reduced speed, then purpose-made tracks at 105–115 BPM with heavy four-on-the-floor kicks, sequenced bass lines and pitched-down vocals. It is filed under techno here because its producers, labels and clubs (R&S, Boccaccio) turned directly into Belgian rave-techno as the tempo rose; it is also a documented precursor of hardcore and of the harder European techno lineage.
genres.name: New Beat

genres.definition: New Orleans jazz is the first ensemble form of jazz: a front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone improvising collectively over a two-beat rhythm section of banjo, tuba or bass, drums and sometimes piano. It formed in New Orleans in the 1900s–1910s from brass-band marches, ragtime and blues, was first recorded in 1917, moved to Chicago in the 1920s and was revived as "Dixieland" or "trad jazz" from the 1940s onward. Collective polyphony and the two-beat bounce separate it from everything that followed.
genres.name: New Orleans Jazz

genres.definition: Nu-disco is the 2000s-onward strand of disco that rebuilds disco, boogie, Italo and space-disco palettes with modern production and DJ-tool structure: kick on every beat at 110–122 BPM, offbeat open hat, synth or played bass with octave and slap figures, funk guitar, analogue arpeggios, sidechain pumping and 16–32-bar intros. It began around Metro Area in New York and the Oslo circle of Lindstrøm and Prins Thomas, grew through edit culture, and reached pop with the 2013–2020 disco revival.
genres.name: Nu-Disco

genres.definition: Nu-skool breaks is the 1998–2008 UK club form of breakbeat: programmed or tightly edited broken drums at 126–134 BPM under a deep sub, Reese or acid bass riff, with techno stabs, electro bleeps and chopped vocals in a house-style DJ arrangement. It replaced big beat's rock samples and song form with bass weight and 16- and 32-bar structure, borrowing production from drum and bass and techno. Bass-led breaks at house-adjacent tempo with DJ structure are the identifiers.
genres.name: Nu-Skool Breaks

genres.definition: Old-school hip-hop is the first recorded era of hip-hop, roughly 1979–1985: party rhymes in simple couplets over disco and funk breaks that were looped by a DJ or re-played by a studio band, later over TR-808 and DMX drum machines. The tempo is faster and the rap less dense than in anything that followed. It ends where the sampler, the chopped break and the dense rhyme scheme begin.
genres.name: Old-School Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Organic house is slow, atmospheric house at roughly 108–120 BPM built from acoustic and sampled instruments of many traditions (oud, duduk, flutes, nylon guitar, hand drums) over a soft kick and minor or modal pads, with sparse chant vocals and long, patient arrangements. It grew out of the 2010s "sunrise" and desert-festival strand of progressive and deep house (Lee Burridge's All Day I Dream, Berlin's Bar 25 circle, Burning Man camps) and was fixed as a category when Beatport introduced "Organic House / Downtempo" in 2020. It is the slow, acoustic-timbred edge of the house family, where house meets downtempo and world music.
genres.name: Organic House

genres.definition: Peak-time techno is the festival and main-room form of techno: 134–142 BPM, a loud and clean kick, a rolling bass line, a big riff hook and an explicit breakdown-drop arc. It is the Drumcode and Awakenings sound of the 2010s and the Charlotte de Witte and Amelie Lens generation of the late 2010s, and Beatport's "Techno (Peak Time / Driving)" category (2020) names it. It borrows dramaturgy from trance and EDM while keeping techno's drum grammar.
genres.name: Peak-Time Techno

genres.definition: Piedmont blues is the country-blues of the southeastern Piedmont plateau (Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia): a fingerpicking style in which the thumb alternates a steady two-pitch bass while the fingers pick a syncopated, ragtime-derived melody, under relaxed singing in major-key and 12-bar forms. Blind Blake, Blind Boy Fuller, Blind Willie McTell, Reverend Gary Davis and the harmonica-guitar duo of Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee define it. Lighter and more dance-oriented than delta-blues, it is the guitar counterpart of ragtime piano.
genres.name: Piedmont Blues

genres.definition: Pop is song-form music made for mass audiences: a lead vocal present through most of a 2–4-minute track, verse/chorus/bridge structure, a chorus hook that repeats, and whatever production palette is current. It is defined by form and function rather than by a sound. Sub-branches include dance-pop, synth-pop, teen pop, power pop, electropop, K-pop, Latin pop, country pop and adult contemporary; most borrow their palette from a neighbouring family.
genres.name: Pop

genres.definition: Pop rock is pop played with a rock band palette: electric guitars, bass and a backbeat kit behind a polished lead vocal and a chorus hook, with songwriting craft and radio fit ahead of riff, solo or attitude. It has existed since the late 1950s as the mainstream middle of the pop–rock spectrum and has no single peak; each decade produces its own version, from Beatles-era beat groups through 1970s and 1980s radio rock to 2000s band-pop. The guitar band is the palette, the pop form is the point.
genres.name: Pop Rock

genres.definition: Post-bop is the acoustic small-group jazz of the mid-1960s onward that absorbed modal and free ideas without giving up the pulse and the head–solos–head form: non-functional harmony, slash and suspended chords, pedal points next to fast changes, odd meters and drummers who stretch and break time. Miles Davis's second quintet (1964–68), Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Andrew Hill, Joe Henderson, Eric Dolphy and the Blue Note roster of 1964–67 are its core; the term is also applied to the acoustic mainstream that followed through the 1980s–1990s.
genres.name: Post-Bop

genres.definition: Post-dubstep is the London umbrella of 2009–2013 for music that took dubstep's sub weight and space but dropped its drop: sparse, broken garage-derived drums at around 130 BPM, piano and Rhodes chords, sung and processed vocals, and song form over DJ form. James Blake, Mount Kimbie, Joy Orbison and Jamie xx are its usual names; Hotflush and Hyperdub its labels. It is a listening genre made by club producers, and the direct ancestor of much alternative R&B.
genres.name: Post-Dubstep

genres.definition: Power pop is the brisk, guitar-crunch end of pop-rock: overdriven rhythm guitar, ringing lead lines, stacked harmonies and a three-minute song with the melodic hooks of the Beatles, the Who and the Beach Boys. Pete Townshend used the term in 1967; the canon formed in the 1970s with Badfinger, Raspberries, Big Star and Cheap Trick and has been revived every decade since (The Knack, Teenage Fanclub, Jellyfish, Fountains of Wayne). Energetic performance under cheerful melody, often with yearning lyrics, is the trademark.
genres.name: Power Pop

genres.definition: Progressive breaks is breakbeat arranged like progressive house and trance: programmed broken drums at 126–132 BPM under long pads, chord progressions, slowly filtered leads and 32-bar builds into a melodic breakdown and drop. It formed in the late 1990s around Hybrid and Way Out West in the UK and had a second home in Melbourne in the 2000s. Pad-led harmony and long-arc dynamics over a broken kick are the identifiers.
genres.name: Progressive Breaks

genres.definition: Progressive EDM is the 2010s mainstage sense of "progressive house", filed under edm-big-room: four-on-the-floor at 126–128 BPM, a pop vocal verse in the breakdown, a snare-roll build and a drop carried by a supersaw lead over a major 4-chord progression. Swedish House Mafia, Avicii, Alesso, Nicky Romero and Zedd define it; Deadmau5 and Eric Prydz supplied the chord-led model. It shares a name but not a form with the 1990s UK progressive house of Sasha, Digweed and Leftfield.
genres.name: Progressive EDM

genres.definition: Progressive house is the long-form, layered strand of house: 122–128 BPM, a house groove with light swing, major or uplifting chord progressions, long atmospheric pads and a slow build across 32-bar phrases toward a breakdown and return. It has two linked meanings: the 1990s UK sound (Leftfield, Guerilla, Sasha and Digweed) that grew out of dub-tinged house and trance, and the 2010s EDM sense (Deadmau5, Eric Prydz, Swedish House Mafia, Avicii) built on chord-led drops and pop vocals. Both share the groove, the chord quality and the patience.
genres.name: Progressive House

genres.definition: Progressive psytrance is the slower, groove-led strand of psytrance: 134–140 BPM, one bass note on the offbeat eighth after every kick, a static harmonic centre and slow, hypnotic builds in place of melodic drops. It formed in Scandinavia, Germany and Denmark around 2000–2004 (Spiral Trax, Digital Structures, Iboga) with minimal-techno and progressive-house habits, and in the 2010s a faster 138–140 "psy-prog" (Ace Ventura, Vini Vici, Astrix) became psytrance's festival mainstream.
genres.name: Progressive Psytrance

genres.definition: Progressive rock is the composed, long-form strand of rock: multi-section suites with changing meters and tempos, classical and jazz devices, keyboard-heavy arrangements (Hammond, Mellotron, Moog) and virtuoso playing, aimed at the album rather than the single. It grew out of British psychedelic-rock in 1967–1969, peaked 1970–1977 (King Crimson, Yes, Genesis, Pink Floyd, Jethro Tull, Emerson Lake & Palmer, Rush), collapsed under punk and returned as neo-prog and, in heavier form, progressive-metal.
genres.name: Progressive Rock

genres.definition: Progressive trance is the slower, layered strand of trance: 128–134 BPM, a rolling or offbeat bass under long pads, chord progressions and plucked or arpeggiated melodies, built up gradually across 32-bar phrases with a moderate breakdown instead of a snare-roll drop. It formed in mid-1990s London beside progressive-house (Platipus, Hooj Choons, Sasha and Digweed) and was re-centred in the 2000s by Anjunabeats and Coldharbour. The patience and the chord-led melody separate it from uplifting trance; the trance bass and straight hats separate it from progressive house.
genres.name: Progressive Trance

genres.definition: Psy-techno is techno built with psytrance tools: psytrance bass onsets between the kicks, squelching psychedelic sound design and dense layering, over a techno kick and techno percussion at 138–148 BPM. It started as a niche hybrid in the 2000s (slower, 128–138), became more dance-floor oriented in the 2010s and reached festival main stages in the 2020s, led by Indira Paganotto and her label ARTCORE. Beatport made it an official sub-genre of Techno (Peak Time / Driving) on 27 January 2026.
genres.name: Psy-Techno

genres.definition: Psybient is the chill-out branch of psychedelic trance filed under ambient: the psytrance palette (resonant acid and FM leads, long delay feedback, swooshing filter FX, ethnic samples) and dub bass at a slow or absent beat. It formed on festival chill-out stages and in the Twisted Records and Ultimae catalogues from the late 1990s. It is more synthetic and effect-heavy than downtempo and more rhythmic than ambient.
genres.name: Psybient

genres.definition: Psychedelic rock is the 1965–1970 strand of rock that set out to reproduce or accompany the LSD experience: modal drones and raga-like leads, fuzz and feedback, studio effects used as instruments (phasing, backwards tape, Leslie vocals), extended improvisation and lyrics about perception. It grew out of garage-rock, folk-rock and blues-rock in San Francisco, London, Los Angeles and Texas, peaked in 1967 and dissolved into progressive-rock, hard-rock, space-rock and krautrock. Neo-psychedelia revived it from the 1980s onward.
genres.name: Psychedelic Rock

genres.definition: Psystyle is a hardstyle hybrid: a distorted, pitched hardstyle kick at 150 BPM with the rolling 1/16 bass line and squelching leads of psytrance laid between the kicks. It appeared in the Dutch raw scene around 2015–2017 (dating uncertain) and sits between rawstyle and full-on psytrance. The rolling bass between hardstyle kicks is the defining trait.
genres.name: Psystyle

genres.definition: Psytrance is the post-1997 umbrella that grew out of goa-trance: a tight dry kick alternating with a plucky single-root bass, few or no sustained melodies, and a dense layer of modulated FX, at roughly 138–148 BPM in its centre and 130–180 across its children. It covers full-on-psytrance (bright, melodic, 142–148), progressive-psytrance (offbeat bass, 134–140), darkpsy (148+, no lead) and the darkpsy offshoots forest-psytrance and hi-tech-psytrance. The chill-out branch is psybient.
genres.name: Psytrance

genres.definition: Punk is fast, short, deliberately simple rock: 1/8-note downstroke guitar on a few chords, a driving kit at 160–220 BPM, shouted vocals, songs under three minutes and a rejection of studio polish and virtuosity. It formed in New York and London in 1974–1977 and branched into hardcore, post-hardcore, pop punk, ska punk, crust, Oi!, anarcho-punk, emo (early) and street punk. Post-punk and new wave moved out toward alternative rock and are not covered here.
genres.name: Punk

genres.definition: Ragga jungle is jungle with a dancehall vocal as the lead element: MC toasting in patois (live or sampled from Jamaican records) rides chopped breaks at 160–170 BPM over a reggae bass line re-pitched to a sub. It peaked in 1994 as jungle's chart face and was the strand the wider scene distanced itself from when it adopted the name drum and bass. The vocal, the reggae bass line and the sound-system FX (sirens, horns, rewinds) are the identifiers.
genres.name: Ragga Jungle

genres.definition: Raggatek is hardtek built on ragga and dancehall vocal hooks and jungle-style breakbeats: 180–195 BPM, alternating between a distorted tekno kick–bass bounce and chopped Amen-style breaks, with pitched-up MC phrases, reggae bass lines and sound-system FX. It is the free-party scene's answer to ragga-jungle, developed in the UK and France in the 2000s and taken to festivals in the 2010s by Mandidextrous and others. "Jungletek" names the same hybrid with the break sections dominant (usage uncertain).
genres.name: Raggatek

genres.definition: Ragtime is composed, notated syncopated piano music from the United States of roughly 1895–1917, built on a march-like left hand in 2/4 and a right-hand melody that "rags" the beat with tied syncopations. It is grouped under jazz as its direct precursor: it supplied the syncopation and the repertoire that early New Orleans bands played, but it is itself not improvised and does not swing. Classic rags are multi-strain forms in major keys, published as sheet music for the parlour piano.
genres.name: Ragtime

genres.definition: Rave techno is the stab-led, anthemic techno of the 1990–1993 European rave boom: a hard four-on-the-floor kick at 130–142 BPM under hoover and piano stabs, sirens and sampled shouts, built for big halls rather than clubs. Belgium (R&S, Ghent), the Netherlands and Germany ("Tekkno", Mayday, Low Spirit) shaped it; the UK took the same sounds onto breakbeats as early-hardcore. Its hoovers and tempo returned in 2020s hard-techno and hard-trance revivals.
genres.name: Rave Techno

genres.definition: Raw techno is loop-based techno with a deliberately lo-fi, saturated, hardware-jammed character: gritty kicks, imperfect percussion loops, hiss and distortion, groove over polish. The label is a 2010s one (L.I.E.S. in New York, the Dutch Bunker and Mord circles, UK producers like Blawan and Truss) and was fixed by Beatport's "Techno (Raw / Deep / Hypnotic)" category in 2020. It is a production aesthetic as much as a style, and its boundary with industrial-techno and minimal-techno is soft; this note describes the centre, not the edges.
genres.name: Raw Techno

genres.definition: Rawstyle is the dark, hard strand of hardstyle: 150–160 BPM, a heavily distorted pitched kick, screech leads instead of supersaw melodies, minor or atonal harmony and spoken or shouted dark vocal fragments. It split from euphoric hardstyle around 2010–2013 as a reaction to the melodic mainstream and took kick design and mood from mainstream-hardcore. The screech and the overdriven kick tail are the defining traits.
genres.name: Rawstyle

genres.definition: Reggae and dancehall are the Jamaican popular-music family: offbeat skank chords, a loud melodic bass line, one-drop or steppers drumming, and vocals from singers and deejays in Patois, built for sound systems. Ska (1960–1966) and rocksteady (1966–1968) led into reggae (1968 onward), roots reggae, dub (the remix practice that became a genre), dancehall (late 1970s onward), digital ragga, lovers rock and the reggaeton and Afrobeats offshoots it seeded abroad.
genres.name: Reggae & Dancehall

genres.definition: Riddim is the minimal, repetitive strand of brostep: one wobble-bass riff of a bar, often in triplets, repeated for 8–16 bars over a bare kick and snare at 140 BPM, with almost no melody, no long build and no layering. It took its name from the Jamaican use of "riddim" for a repeating instrumental, formed online among UK and European producers in 2012–2015 and peaked on the US festival circuit in 2016–2019. Repetition is the hook.
genres.name: Riddim

genres.definition: Rock is band music centred on electric guitar, bass, drum kit and a sung lead, in verse/chorus songs driven by riffs and a backbeat. It grew out of 1950s rock and roll and 1960s blues-based and beat groups and splits into many branches: hard rock, psychedelic, progressive, glam, alternative and indie, grunge, post-punk, shoegaze, emo and arena rock. Metal and punk started inside rock and are treated as separate families here.
genres.name: Rock

genres.definition: Rock and roll is the 1950s dance music that rock grew from: blues and rhythm-and-blues song forms played at jump tempo by small bands of electric guitar, piano, saxophone, bass and drums, with a hard snare backbeat and a sung lead aimed at teenagers. The 12-bar cycle, boogie bass and triplet piano come from blues, jump-blues and boogie-woogie; the vocal styles mix rhythm-and-blues, gospel and country. It peaked 1955–1959 and splits into rockabilly (its country-leaning Memphis strand) and, via the 1960s beat groups, into rock proper.
genres.name: Rock and Roll

genres.definition: Rockabilly is the country-leaning Memphis strand of rock-and-roll: a trio or quartet of electric lead guitar, acoustic rhythm guitar and slapped upright bass, with or without a small drum kit, playing hillbilly boogie and blues cycles at high tempo under a hiccuping vocal soaked in slapback echo. It formed at Sun Records in 1954–1956, faded by 1960 and returned through 1970s–80s revival scenes in the US and UK that fed psychobilly.
genres.name: Rockabilly

genres.definition: Romanian minimal is the slow, swung, bass-led strand of minimal-techno that grew around Bucharest's a:rpia:r label (Rhadoo, Raresh, Petre Inspirescu) and the Sunwaves festival (Mamaia, 2007–2025): 122–127 BPM, a clean kick under a rolling melodic sub, micro-sampled percussion with house swing, dubby chord fragments and very long, slowly mutating arrangements. It is house-rooted minimal rather than techno-rooted, and the only minimal strand that stayed a mass club culture after 2010.
genres.name: Romanian Minimal

genres.definition: Schranz is the German strand of hard-techno from the late 1990s and 2000s: 150–165 BPM, a hard and comparatively dry kick, and looped, distorted, compressed machine percussion that runs in constant motion with no melody, no vocals and no breakdown-drop arc. The word was coined by Frankfurt DJ Chris Liebing (accounts place it in 1994 at the Boy Records store or in 1997 on a Cologne radio show; its etymology is uncertain and probably imitative of the crunchy loop sound). It is loop techno pushed to maximum density and tempo.
genres.name: Schranz

genres.definition: Slap house is the late-2010s radio-house strand under edm-big-room: 122–126 BPM, a punchy kick, and a plucked, sidechained "slap" bass line that plays a syncopated minor melody as the hook, under a heavily processed pop vocal in a sparse three-minute form. It grew from Brazil's "Brazilian bass" (Alok, Vintage Culture, 2015–2017) and reached global radio through Dynoro & Gigi D'Agostino's "In My Mind" (2018) and Imanbek's "Roses" remix (2019); the name "slap house" attached around 2019–2020. The bass is the melody; everything else stays out of its way.
genres.name: Slap House

genres.definition: Smooth jazz is the radio-format strand of jazz that grew from the softer side of 1970s fusion and jazz-funk: a saxophone or clean guitar melody over programmed or lightly played straight-8th grooves, synth pads and electric bass, in pop song forms at 75–105 BPM with short melodic solos and a polished, compressed mix. It was codified by the "new adult contemporary" radio format launched in Los Angeles in 1987 and peaked in the 1990s with Kenny G, Dave Koz, Boney James, Fourplay and the GRP label. US radio and Billboard call it "contemporary jazz"; this atlas keeps that id for the modern creative umbrella (contemporary-jazz).
genres.name: Smooth Jazz

genres.definition: Sophisti-pop is the polished, jazz-and-soul-inflected British pop of the mid-1980s: jazz-extended chords on electric piano and DX7, fretless bass, saxophone, lavish keyboard arrangements and a cool, restrained vocal, produced to a high gloss. It developed out of the new wave era — Roxy Music's *Avalon* (1982) is the model — and peaked with Sade, Prefab Sprout, The Style Council, The Blue Nile, Simply Red, Everything but the Girl, Swing Out Sister and Scritti Politti before declining in the 1990s; the term itself was coined after the fact. Restraint is the point: nothing is belted, nothing distorts.
genres.name: Sophisti-Pop

genres.definition: Soul blues is blues sung and produced like soul: a gospel-trained lead vocal over a soul rhythm section with horns, organ and backing vocals, keeping 12-bar and 8-bar blues cycles and blues lyric themes. It formed in the 1960s when Bobby "Blue" Bland, Little Milton, Johnnie Taylor and Albert King recorded for Duke, Checker and Stax with soul bands, and peaked in the 1980s on Malaco Records (Z. Z. Hill's "Down Home Blues", 1982), where it became the house music of Black Southern radio and the Chitlin' Circuit. It sits between memphis-blues, southern-soul and contemporary-blues.
genres.name: Soul Blues

genres.definition: Soul jazz is the gospel- and blues-rooted, groove-first jazz of the late 1950s and 1960s: Hammond organ trios and gospel piano trios playing 12-bar blues, church vamps and riff tunes with a shuffle or backbeat, short solos and a jukebox-friendly length. It split off from hard bop through Jimmy Smith, Horace Silver's funkier tunes and Cannonball Adderley's quintet, produced crossover hits ("The In Crowd", "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy", "Alligator Bogaloo") and was the direct ancestor of jazz-funk and the acid-jazz revival.
genres.name: Soul Jazz

genres.definition: Soul, R&B and funk form one African-American family of groove-based vocal music: gospel singing technique over secular songs, syncopated rhythm sections and horn or keyboard arrangements. Rhythm and blues (1940s) led into soul (late 1950s–1960s), funk (mid-1960s) and the disco, boogie, quiet storm, new jack swing, neo-soul and contemporary R&B lines that followed. The sung, melismatic lead and the groove-first rhythm section hold across all of them.
genres.name: Soul, R&B & Funk

genres.definition: Soulful house is house played like a soul record: a live or live-sounding band palette (Rhodes, bass guitar, horns, strings), extended jazz voicings and a gospel-rooted lead vocal over a 120–126 BPM groove. It is the 2000s continuation of New York and New Jersey garage-house, named and marketed by labels such as Defected, Vega Records, Yoruba and Objektivity, and it became the dominant house style in South Africa before afro-house grew out of it. Musicianship and the singer matter more than the drum programming.
genres.name: Soulful House

genres.definition: Southern hip-hop is the regional family of hip-hop from the US South, centred on Atlanta, Houston, New Orleans, Memphis and Miami: drum-machine production built on the 808 kick and its sub tail, chanted and call-and-response hooks, and a slower or half-time feel under a drawled delivery. It developed from the late 1980s outside the New York–Los Angeles axis and has dominated mainstream rap since the mid-2000s through crunk, snap and above all trap. Its drums are programmed, not sampled, and its hooks are built for the club.
genres.name: Southern Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Space disco is the late-1970s science-fiction strand of disco, mostly from France, Italy and Germany: a disco rhythm section with an offbeat open hat under Moog arpeggios, vocoder chants, laser and swoosh FX, orchestral strings and long instrumental passages, themed on space travel in the wake of "Star Wars" (1977). Space's "Magic Fly", Cerrone's "Supernature" and Dee D. Jackson's "Automatic Lover" define it. The name was reused in the 2000s for the Norwegian long-form disco of Lindstrøm and Prins Thomas, which this atlas files under nu-disco.
genres.name: Space Disco

genres.definition: Speed garage is the first London strand of uk-garage: US garage house pitched up to 130–135 BPM, kept on a four-on-the-floor kick, and fitted with the warped, sliding sub bass and time-stretched vocals of jungle. It peaked in 1997–1998, gave way to the skipping kick of 2-step, and its 4/4 template resurfaced a decade later as bassline. The kick stays on every beat; the bass does the moving.
genres.name: Speed Garage

genres.definition: Speed metal is heavy-metal played fast: 170–200 BPM with a continuous kick drive, while keeping heavy metal's melodic riffs, clean high vocals and harmonised solos. It names the early-1980s moment between NWOBHM and thrash — Motörhead, Judas Priest's fast songs, Accept, Exciter, Anvil, early Helloween and Running Wild — and the term is used loosely for bands that sit between thrash-metal (which shouts and palm-mutes) and power-metal (which adds keys and major-key anthems). Boundaries are fuzzy; many sources treat it as a transitional style rather than a lasting scene.
genres.name: Speed Metal

genres.definition: Speedcore is hardcore above roughly 300 BPM: a clipped kick repeated so fast that it reads as a buzz or pitched tone, blast-beat bursts, cartoon and horror samples and abrupt stop-start edits, with no danceable quarter-note pulse. It emerged in the early to mid-1990s out of terror and gabber (Moby's 1,000-BPM "Thousand" from 1993 is the usual novelty landmark), and it has strands in Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, the US and Japan; splittercore (600+) and extratone (1,000+) are its faster tiers. The `bpm` field is left null: the schema caps tempo below 400 and DJ software halves or fails on this material, so the kick onset rate is the usable measure.
genres.name: Speedcore

genres.definition: Surf rock is the early-1960s Southern Californian strand of rock: clean Fender guitars through outboard spring reverb playing fast tremolo-picked melodies and glissandi over rolling drums, mostly instrumental, at 150–190 BPM. A parallel vocal strand (The Beach Boys, Jan and Dean) stacks falsetto harmonies over the same beat. It grew out of rock-and-roll and rockabilly instrumentals around 1961, peaked 1962–1964 and was cut off by the British Invasion, returning in several revivals.
genres.name: Surf Rock

genres.definition: Swamp blues is the slow, laid-back blues of the Baton Rouge area recorded by J. D. Miller in Crowley, Louisiana for Excello Records from the mid-1950s: Jimmy Reed's lazy shuffle slowed further, with harmonica, tremolo guitar, heavy echo and improvised percussion. Slim Harpo, Lightnin' Slim, Lazy Lester, Lonesome Sundown, Silas Hogan and Whispering Smith are its core. It took the chicago-blues of Reed and absorbed local Cajun, zydeco and New Orleans R&B feel; British bands covered it heavily in the 1960s.
genres.name: Swamp Blues

genres.definition: Swing is the dance-oriented jazz of the 1930s and early 1940s: a 4/4 rhythm section with walking bass, four-to-the-bar guitar and hi-hat on 2 and 4 under riff-based arrangements and single soloists, played at tempos people could Lindy Hop to. It is both a rhythmic feel (long-short 1/8s with a strong four) and a period style; the style covers big bands and small combos alike. Sectional riffs, walking bass and a steady dance pulse are its fingerprints.
genres.name: Swing

genres.definition: Synth-pop is pop whose palette is synthesizers, sequencers and drum machines in place of a guitar band: a synth lead riff as the hook, sequenced bass, programmed drums and a cool, often deadpan vocal in verse/chorus form. It formed in Germany, Japan and the UK around 1977–1980 out of Kraftwerk, disco and new wave, peaked commercially in the UK in 1981–82 (The Human League, Depeche Mode, OMD, Soft Cell) and shaped house and techno in turn. Its 2000s–2010s descendants are covered under electropop.
genres.name: Synth-Pop

genres.definition: Synthwave is the 2000s–2010s revival strand under electro that recreates 1980s film-score and synth-pop sounds: LinnDrum kits and gated-reverb snares, sidechained sawtooth bass on straight 1/8, Juno pads, DX7 bells and arpeggios at 80–120 BPM, mostly instrumental. It grew out of the French electro scene around Kavinsky and the Valerie collective (2006–2009), spread through YouTube channels and Bandcamp, and reached a mass audience with the "Drive" soundtrack (2011). Listening and driving music more than club music.
genres.name: Synthwave

genres.definition: Tech house is the dry, bass-riff-driven strand of house: 124–128 BPM, a tight kick, swung percussion, a repeating melodic bass line as the hook and chopped vocals, with techno's sparse harmony replacing house's chords. It formed in mid-1990s London as DJs blended Chicago house with Detroit techno, and since the 2010s it has been the largest club and Beatport category. The groove is the bass line; everything else is texture.
genres.name: Tech House

genres.definition: Tech trance is the dark, percussive strand of trance: 138–142 BPM, a hard clean kick over a rolling bass, a dense techno-derived percussion loop and short minor-key riffs in place of a long melody, with a 16–32-bar breakdown that keeps the tension rather than releasing it. Dutch producers (Marco V, Sander van Doorn, Marcel Woods) defined it in the 2000s and UK labels (Outburst, Damaged, VII) carried it through the 2010s. It borrows techno's percussion grammar and hard-trance's drive while keeping trance's bass and arrangement.
genres.name: Tech Trance

genres.definition: Technical death metal is death-metal built for complexity: odd meters, frequent tempo and meter changes, sweep-picked arpeggios, dissonant harmony, audible bass counterpoint and drumming that changes pattern every few bars. It formed in 1989–1993 around Death's later albums, Atheist, Cynic and Pestilence in Florida and the Netherlands, took its dissonant strand from Gorguts and Cryptopsy in Quebec, and was reset in the 2000s by Necrophagist, then Obscura, Beyond Creation and Archspire. It borders progressive-metal on the clean side and brutal-death-metal on the slam side.
genres.name: Technical Death Metal

genres.definition: Techno is machine-made electronic dance music built on a four-on-the-floor kick, repetition and timbre rather than song form. It emerged in Detroit in the mid-1980s from electro, funk and Chicago house, and became the backbone of European club culture from the 1990s onward. Tracks are tools for DJs: long, loop-based, percussion-led, with melody and vocals kept minimal or absent.
genres.name: Techno

genres.definition: Techstep is the cold, programmed strand of drum-and-bass that formed in London in 1996–1998: dry two-step drums at 168–175 BPM under a sustained, distorted Reese bass, with industrial textures and sci-fi dialogue instead of reggae or soul samples. It replaced the sampled break with the drum machine and the sub with a mid-range bass, and it is the ancestor of darkstep and neurofunk. The sustained distorted Reese is the trait that names it.
genres.name: Techstep

genres.definition: Tekk (also Hardtekk, Tekkno) is fast, harsh German hard-techno: a heavily distorted kick at 160–180 BPM under spoken quotes, film or meme audio and bootlegged snippets of pop and schlager hits, in simple, repetitive loops. It is mainly produced in Germany, has a strong festival and TikTok presence, and is a different scene from the French free-party hardtek despite the near-identical name. Sources disagree on its origin (late 1990s or early 2000s, often placed in eastern Germany); treat the history as uncertain.
genres.name: Tekk

genres.definition: Terrorcore (terror) is the harshest four-on-the-floor strand of hardcore below speedcore tempo: roughly 200–250 BPM (range uncertain), a kick clipped to a near-square wave that drowns every other layer, horror and violence samples, noise stabs and a flat, breakdown-free structure. It formed in the mid-1990s in Rotterdam, Frankfurt, New York and Newcastle (Australia) as gabber's extreme wing and persists as a small scene alongside uptempo and speedcore. Clipped kick plus horror samples plus no drop arc at 200+ BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Terrorcore

genres.definition: Texas blues is the guitar-led strand of electric-blues from Dallas, Houston and later Austin: single-string lead lines with swing phrasing and wide bends over a shuffle, with horn charts in the Houston big-band line and little harmonica. It runs from the acoustic Dallas and Houston singers (Blind Lemon Jefferson, Lightnin' Hopkins) through T-Bone Walker, Clarence "Gatemouth" Brown, Albert Collins, Freddie King and Johnny Winter to the Austin revival of Stevie Ray Vaughan, Jimmie Vaughan and the Fabulous Thunderbirds. T-Bone Walker is the shared root with west-coast-blues.
genres.name: Texas Blues

genres.definition: Thrash metal is the fast, percussive branch of metal that formed in 1981–1985 when NWOBHM riffing met hardcore-punk tempo and attitude: palm-muted, down-picked 1/16 riffs with chromatic motion, a skank or double-kick drum drive at 170–210 BPM, shouted vocals and fast solos. The Bay Area (Metallica, Exodus, Testament), Los Angeles (Slayer, Megadeth), New York (Anthrax, Overkill) and the German Ruhr (Kreator, Sodom, Destruction) are the core scenes. death-metal and black-metal grew out of its extreme end; groove-metal out of its slow end.
genres.name: Thrash Metal

genres.definition: Traditional pop is pre-rock pop: the Great American Songbook repertoire of Berlin, Gershwin, Porter and Rodgers sung by crooners and band singers over orchestras or swing bands, roughly from the 1920s to the arrival of rock and roll in the mid-1950s. The song is a 32-bar refrain, the vocal is the centre, the backing is arranged rather than played as a groove. The style survives as "standards" through Sinatra, Bennett and later revivalists.
genres.name: Traditional Pop

genres.definition: Trance is melodic four-on-the-floor electronic dance music at roughly 128–150 BPM, centred on sustained lead melodies, chord progressions and a breakdown-build-drop arc that delivers the melody at full force. It grew out of Frankfurt techno and acid house around 1990–1993, then split into uplifting, progressive, vocal, psychedelic and hard strands. Where techno is about texture and pressure, trance is about melody and release.
genres.name: Trance

genres.definition: Trance techno is 2020s techno with trance on top: techno drums and a techno low end (rumble or one-note sub, straight 1/16 hats) under sustained trance leads, supersaws, acid-trance arpeggios and chord-carrying breakdowns, at 140–152 BPM. It is the techno side of the 2020s trance revival: SoundCloud reported trance uploads up 29 % in its first Music Intelligence Report (2025), Beatport split trance into "Main Floor" and "Raw / Deep / Hypnotic" in May 2023, and Armin van Buuren and Adam Beyer released "Techno Trance" in September 2025. The bass decides it: trance bass makes it hard-trance or tech-trance, a bouncing offbeat bass makes it hard-bounce.
genres.name: Trance Techno

genres.definition: Trap is the Atlanta-born form of southern-hip-hop that became the default grammar of rap worldwide in the 2010s: a half-time grid notated at 130–150 BPM with the snare on every second beat, a tuned 808 sub that slides between notes, dense 1/16 and triplet hi-hat rolls and sparse minor-key motifs, under a rap that ranges from deadpan to Auto-Tuned melody. The name comes from the "trap house" of the drug trade that early lyrics described; the sound was fixed by Shawty Redd, Zaytoven, Lex Luger and 808 Mafia between 2003 and 2012. The hats and the 808 are the genre.
genres.name: Trap

genres.definition: Tribal house is house whose groove is carried by layered hand percussion rather than by chords, bass line or vocal: congas, bongos, djembe, timbales and toms in syncopated loops over a punchy kick at 126–130 BPM, with chants instead of songs and little or no harmony. It formed in New York in the early 1990s around Junior Vasquez at the Sound Factory, Danny Tenaglia at Twilo and the Tribal America label, and became a 2000s staple of circuit parties, Ibiza and Spanish clubs. Its faster, colder sibling is tribal-techno.
genres.name: Tribal House

genres.definition: Tribal techno is techno whose groove is carried by dense, syncopated hand-drum percussion (congas, bongos, toms, shakers, cowbells) rather than by synth hooks or kick pressure. It peaked in the 2000s in the UK (Ben Sims, Mark Broom), Spain (Cristian Varela and the Madrid and Barcelona club scenes) and Italy, borrowing from tribal house and from african and latin percussion traditions. Its faster, kick-heavier descendant is hardgroove; the boundary between the two is soft and partly a matter of era and tempo.
genres.name: Tribal Techno

genres.definition: Trip-hop is the dark, song-based Bristol strand of ambient-downtempo: slowed hip-hop breaks at 60–100 BPM under minor-key samples, dub bass, scratches and, in its best-known form, soulful female vocals. Massive Attack, Portishead and Tricky defined it between 1991 and 1995; the press term came from Mixmag in 1994 for the instrumental Mo' Wax records of DJ Shadow and others. It is hip-hop production with the MC replaced by atmosphere and a singer.
genres.name: Trip-Hop

genres.definition: Tropical house is the slow, bright pop strand of house from 2013–2017: 108–118 BPM, a soft kick, marimba, steel-drum, kalimba or pan-flute leads, saxophone and acoustic guitar, and a full pitch-corrected pop vocal in a major key. Kygo (Bergen), Robin Schulz and Felix Jaehn (Germany), Lost Frequencies (Belgium) and Thomas Jack (Australia, who coined the tag) took it from SoundCloud remixes to global charts, and the chart press often called it deep house. It is pop with a house kick and a holiday palette; the instrumental hook after the chorus is its signature.
genres.name: Tropical House

genres.definition: 2-step is the uk-garage strand defined by its kick: the second or third kick of the bar is dropped, so the groove lurches over shuffled hats and a snare on 2 and 4 at 132–138 BPM. It formed in London in 1997–1998 out of speed garage and pitched-up garage house, carried sung R&B hooks into the UK charts in 1999–2001, and its dark instrumental end became grime and dubstep. The skipping kick, not the tempo, is the identity.
genres.name: 2-Step Garage

genres.definition: UK bass is the umbrella name for the London and Bristol club music of roughly 2008–2013 that sat between uk-garage, grime, dubstep, UK funky, house and techno without being any of them: instrumental, percussive, bass-led tracks at 128–138 BPM with cold grime-derived synths and DJ-friendly structure. The name is a filing label more than a sound, which is why its tempo window is wide. It is the instrumental successor of UK funky and the club-facing twin of post-dubstep.
genres.name: UK Bass

genres.definition: UK drill is the London rebuild of Chicago drill, formed in Brixton and South London from about 2012: the same half-time 808 grid at 138–145 notated and the same deadpan violence lyrics, but with a syncopated kick pattern, a snare that skips or delays the half-time position and a gliding 808 sub bass sliding between notes. Producers such as 808 Melo, AXL Beats, Carns Hill and M1OnTheBeat fixed the drum grammar in 2016–2018; it was exported back to Brooklyn and became the dominant UK rap style of the late 2010s. Its drums carry the DNA of grime and UK garage.
genres.name: UK Drill

genres.definition: UK funky is the London strand of uk-garage at 128–132 BPM that pulls house's tempo and soca's syncopation together: the snare or clap leaves beats 2 and 4, congas and tribal percussion fill the bar, and sung R&B hooks or grime-trained MCs sit on top. It formed in 2006–2008 on Rinse FM and in East and South London clubs, peaked in 2008–2009 and fed its instrumental side into UK bass. The displaced snare is the fingerprint.
genres.name: UK Funky

genres.definition: UK garage is London's 1990s reworking of US garage house into a shuffled, bass-heavy style at 130–138 BPM: a skipping two-step kick, swung hats, pitched-up R&B vocals and a syncopated sub bass. It covers speed garage (four-on-the-floor at 130+, 1996–1998), 2-step (kick dropping beats, 1998–2002) and later bassline and UK funky. It is the parent of grime and dubstep and a sibling of house in sound.
genres.name: UK Garage

genres.definition: UK hardcore is the post-2000 continuation of happy-hardcore inside the hardcore family: 170–180 BPM, a punchy kick, a bouncing offbeat bass, supersaw leads carrying a sung melody and trance-style breakdowns and builds, with the 1990s piano riffs, rave stabs and breakbeat layer dropped. The name replaced "happy hardcore" in the UK scene around 2000–2003 (uncertain) and the sound peaked with the Clubland X-Treme Hardcore compilations in the mid- to late 2000s. Supersaw melody plus offbeat bass at 170+ BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: UK Hardcore

genres.definition: Uplifting trance is the anthemic core of trance: 136–140 BPM, a supersaw lead melody over a chord progression, a sidechained rolling bass, and a long kick-less breakdown that builds with a snare roll into a euphoric drop. It took shape in the Netherlands, Germany and the UK superclubs around 1996–1999 and was the commercial face of trance from 1998 to 2003; since the late 2000s a "138" revival (FSOE, Who's Afraid of 138?!) keeps it as the reference form. The breakdown-build-drop arc centred on the melody is the genre.
