genres.name: Uplifting Trance

genres.definition: Uptempo hardcore is the accelerated 2010s wing of mainstream-hardcore: 195–225 BPM (range uncertain), a short heavily distorted kick played in doubled 1/8, triplet and bouncing patterns with pitch jumps inside the bar, screech stabs and shouted or meme vocals, with short or no breakdowns. It grew from the Dutch and Belgian hardcore scene around 2013–2016 (uncertain) and took festival mainstages in the 2020s. Sustained doubled-kick density above 190 BPM is the fingerprint.
genres.name: Uptempo Hardcore

genres.definition: Vaporwave is a sample-based internet genre filed under ambient-downtempo: 1980s and 1990s pop, R&B, smooth jazz, muzak and city pop slowed, pitched down, chopped into loops and drenched in reverb, with consumer culture and nostalgia as its subject. It emerged online in 2010–2011 from Chuck Person's "Eccojams Vol. 1", James Ferraro's "Far Side Virtual" and Macintosh Plus's "Floral Shoppe", as an ironic offshoot of chillwave. Nothing is newly performed; the material is the recording itself.
genres.name: Vaporwave

genres.definition: Vocal house is house built around a full sung song: a lead vocal with verse, chorus and ad-libs over a 122–128 BPM groove of punchy kick, clap, synth stabs and pads. The term covers the diva-led club and chart house of roughly 1989–1999 (Robin S, CeCe Peniston, Crystal Waters, Ultra Naté) and every later house record whose vocal is the hook rather than a sample. It is a descriptor as much as a style, so this note describes the chart-era centre and separates it from the gospel-rooted garage-house and the live-band soulful-house.
genres.name: Vocal House

genres.definition: Vocal jazz is jazz with the singer as the lead voice for most of the track: standards and originals delivered with swing phrasing, melodic paraphrase and improvisation (scat, vocalese) over a jazz rhythm section or big band, with at most a chorus or two for instrumental solos. It runs from Louis Armstrong and Bessie Smith through Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Frank Sinatra and Nat King Cole to Cassandra Wilson, Kurt Elling, Gregory Porter and Cécile McLorin Salvant. The swing rhythm section and the liberty taken with the written tune separate it from pop singing of the same songs.
genres.name: Vocal Jazz

genres.definition: Vocal trance is trance built around a full sung song: a verse carried by the breakdown, a chorus whose melody the supersaw lead restates in the drop, over the uplifting or progressive trance groove at 134–140 BPM. It broke through in 1998–2001 (Delerium's "Silence" remixes, Fragma, Chicane) and was the house style of Armada, Anjunabeats and Black Hole through the 2000s, with recurring guest singers (Emma Hewitt, Zoë Johnston, Susana, Justine Suissa). The vocal is the hook; the trance arrangement serves it.
genres.name: Vocal Trance

genres.definition: West Coast blues is the jazz-inflected strand of electric-blues that formed in Los Angeles and the Oakland–San Francisco Bay Area in the 1940s, when Texas and Louisiana migrants met the city's swing and cocktail-combo scene: piano-and-guitar combos with sax, 9th-chord comping, a relaxed swing and crooned vocals. T-Bone Walker, Pee Wee Crayton, Lowell Fulson, Charles Brown (with Johnny Moore's Three Blazers), Floyd Dixon, Amos Milburn and Percy Mayfield are its core. It shares T-Bone Walker with texas-blues and the horn riffs of jump-blues, but plays both slower and smoother.
genres.name: West Coast Blues

genres.definition: West Coast hip-hop is the California strand of hip-hop: funk-rooted production built on replayed or synthesised bass lines, high synth leads, talkbox and drum machines rather than chopped samples, under a slower, more relaxed flow at 90–100 BPM. It covers the 1980s Los Angeles electro-rap and early gangsta records, the G-funk of 1992–1996, the Bay Area mobb and hyphy scenes, and the 2010s ratchet and Compton revival. Its sound is played and synthesised where the East Coast's is sampled.
genres.name: West Coast Hip-Hop

genres.definition: Wonky is the off-grid, detuned strand of late-2000s bass music: drums deliberately placed away from the quantised grid, synth leads bent and detuned until they wobble, heavy sub bass and a head-nod backbeat, at either hip-hop tempo or 140 half-time. Wikipedia dates its emergence to 2006 and names Joker, Rustie, Hudson Mohawke, Zomby and Flying Lotus; Glasgow's "aquacrunk" and Bristol's "purple sound" are its regional names. It sits under dubstep because its 140 strand and its labels (Hyperdub, Planet Mu) came from that scene, but half of it is instrumental hip-hop. The term is a critics' word that most of the artists rejected.
genres.name: Wonky

genres.definition: Wonky techno is the irregular, humorous, hardware-jammed techno of the mid-1990s Edinburgh–Brighton circle: Neil Landstrumm, Tobias Schmidt, Cristian Vogel, Si Begg, Subhead and Dave Tarrida, released on Peacefrog, Tresor, Mosquito and their own labels. Lurching off-grid percussion, bent pitches and abrupt structures sit inside a four-on-the-floor kick at 130–138 BPM. The name began as a record-shop shelf category. It is not the 2008 bass-music wonky of Rustie and Hudson Mohawke.
genres.name: Wonky Techno

genres.definition: World-regional is the catch-all family for regional and traditional musics outside the other families: European traditions (flamenco, fado, chanson, rebetiko, Balkan brass, klezmer, Celtic and Nordic folk, polka, tarantella), Middle Eastern and North African (Arabic classical and pop, Turkish, Persian, Gnawa, raï), South Asian (Hindustani and Carnatic classical, qawwali, Bollywood film song, bhangra), East and Southeast Asian (Chinese traditional, gagaku, J-pop and K-pop-adjacent traditional, gamelan), Oceanian and Indigenous musics, plus the "world music" fusion market of the 1980s onward. Sub-Saharan music is african, Latin American music is latin and Anglophone folk is folk-country. Common ground is only negative: regional language, regional instruments, scales and meters that fall outside the 12-tone, 4/4, drum-kit norm. Tempo is not a defining property.
genres.name: World & Regional

tags.meaning: "Acid" always means a TB-303 or clone line with a moving resonant filter, but it is attached to music from 118 to 190 BPM. Which genre the track belongs to depends on the drums and tempo around the acid line and on how much of the track the line occupies.
tags.name: Acid

resolution.acid-house: the 303 line over a swung house drum pattern with claps, often vocals, 118–126 BPM.
resolution.acid-techno: the 303 line is present for most of the track over straight techno drums, one root throughout, 135–145 BPM.
resolution.acid-trance: the 303 framed in a trance arrangement with a 16–32-bar kick-less breakdown, pads and chord changes, 135–142 BPM.
resolution.acidcore: distorted, often layered 303 lines over a distorted kick with a tekno bass bounce, lo-fi master, 160–180 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: a short acid stab as hook over a rumbling kick with riser breakdowns, 148–158 BPM; the 303 occupies less than half of the track.
resolution.psy-techno: acid squelches among psychedelic FX over psytrance bass onsets and a techno kick, 138–148 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport's store category for the harder styles. Track pages show sub-genres such as Hardstyle, Frenchcore, UK / Happy Hardcore, Hard House and Neo Rave under it. "Neo Rave" was added on 18 April 2024; when the parent name gained "/ Neo Rave" is not documented (uncertain). The category is a catch-all for everything with a hard-dance kick or hardcore tempo.
tags.name: Hard Dance / Hardcore / Neo Rave (Beatport)

resolution.frenchcore: dominant clipped hardcore kick with screech or hoover leads, 190–220 BPM.
resolution.happy-hardcore: clean kick, piano chords and sung vocals, often a breakbeat layer, 165–180 BPM.
resolution.hard-house: offbeat bass stab under a cleaner house kick with claps, hoovers or trance stabs, 145–155 BPM.
resolution.hardstyle: pitched kick tail or reverse bass that follows the melody, euphoric or vocal breakdowns, 150–155 BPM.
resolution.mainstream-hardcore: Dutch hardcore kick with melodic leads and MC vocals, 160–180 BPM.
resolution.rawstyle: pitched, distorted kick tail with screech riffs in the drop and a reverse-bass intro, 150–160 BPM.
resolution.uk-hardcore: the 2000s UK descendant of happy hardcore with trance-style leads, 165–180 BPM.
resolution.uptempo-hardcore: extremely distorted, dominant kick with Dutch hardcore grammar, 190–220 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport reinstated "Hard Techno" as a store genre in mid-2020 (reported as 28 July 2020; the press release file sits in a December 2020 upload folder), filled from its two techno categories created in February 2020. Purchased files carry it in the genre field, so it arrives in DJ software and in libraries as-is. It is a store bucket for everything techno-room and fast, not a sound: a single Hard Techno chart mixes rumble techno, schranz edits, bounce, trance leads, groove and acid.
tags.name: Hard Techno (Beatport)

resolution.acid-techno: a TB-303 resonant line present for most of the track over straight techno drums, 130–150 BPM.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab alternating with the kick, pitched hooks, modern master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: rumble tail under a distorted kick, 1/16 hat rolls, short hook, riser breakdowns, 148–165 BPM.
resolution.hardgroove: swung, syncopated hand-drum percussion and chopped vocal shouts over a punchy, decaying kick, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.industrial-techno: sustained noise layers and long reverb tails, distorted dry kick, 130–145 BPM, no drop dramaturgy.
resolution.schranz: dense distorted percussion loops in constant motion over a dry kick, no vocals, no long kick-less sections, 150–165 BPM.
resolution.tekk: dominant distorted kick with spoken quotes or bootleg snippets in simple loops, often 165+ BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: static sub or rumble under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport's store genre for leftfield, post-punk-, disco- and new-wave-rooted club music; it carries the sub-genre "Dark Disco". Until September 2019 it shared a category with Nu Disco ("Nu Disco / Indie Dance"); since 29 September 2026 its heavier, club-focused side moved to the new "Indie Tech" genre, so older files tagged Indie Dance can also be Indie Tech material.
tags.name: Indie Dance (Beatport)

resolution.dark-disco: minor or modal melodies, gloomy synths and guitars over a chugging, lightly swung bass, 112–124 BPM.
resolution.ebm: rigid sequenced bass and shouted vocals over drum machines, 115–130 BPM.
resolution.electroclash: song form with deadpan vocal choruses and synth-pop or punk hooks, 122–130 BPM.
resolution.italo-disco: bright 1980s synth-pop melodies with sung or vocoded choruses and octave bass, 118–126 BPM.
resolution.nu-disco: bright, major, funk-bass driven disco revival with a live-band feel, 112–122 BPM.
resolution.synthwave: 1980s film-score palette, gated snares, often half-time feel, 100–118 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport launched "Indie Tech" as a standalone genre on 29 September 2026, splitting the heavier, polished, peak-time side out of Indie Dance: punchy drums, prominent basslines and bold synth hooks, influenced by Tech House, Melodic House & Techno, Bass House and Mainstage. Named artists include Adam Ten, Mita Gami, Vintage Culture and Oliver Koletzki; labels include Maccabi House, Stil Vor Talent, Get Physical and Diynamic. Beatport gives no tempo; the resolution below is an assessment (uncertain).
tags.name: Indie Tech (Beatport)

resolution.afro-house: syncopated afro percussion and chants under melodic pads, 120–125 BPM.
resolution.bass-house: distorted, wobbling mid-bass riffs over a house groove, 125–128 BPM.
resolution.melodic-techno: minor-key arpeggio lead over straight drums with cinematic breakdowns, 120–126 BPM.
resolution.progressive-edm: big-room build with a snare roll and a melodic mainstage drop, 126–128 BPM.
resolution.tech-house: repeating bass-riff hook, vocal chops and house-style 8-bar builds, 124–128 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport added "Melodic House & Techno" on 20 March 2018, pulling in tracks previously filed under Techno, Deep House, Tech House and Electronica. It is the store home of the Afterlife and Innervisions sound and of melodic progressive house; Organic House / Downtempo got its own category in June 2020.
tags.name: Melodic House & Techno (Beatport)

resolution.afro-house: syncopated afro percussion and chants under melodic pads, 120–125 BPM.
resolution.deep-house: sustained chords or pads with house swing and often sung vocals, 118–124 BPM.
resolution.melodic-techno: minor-key arpeggio lead over straight techno drums with long cinematic breakdowns, 120–126 BPM.
resolution.organic-house: acoustic instrument lead over a soft kick and hand percussion, 108–120 BPM (files from before June 2020).
resolution.progressive-house: house-derived groove with swung percussion, major or uplifting chords and long builds, 122–128 BPM.

tags.meaning: A Beatport store genre for reduced, groove-led club music between techno and house; its introduction date is not documented (track pages carry it for releases from at least 2013). It mixes techno-rooted minimal, Romanian-style minimal, microhouse and the "deep tech" end of tech house.
tags.name: Minimal / Deep Tech (Beatport)

resolution.deep-house: sustained chords or pads, often sung vocals, warm low end, 118–124 BPM.
resolution.microhouse: glitchy cut-up funk micro-samples with house swing and harmonic fragments, 120–126 BPM.
resolution.minimal-techno: straight grid, kick-dominant, synthetic clicks and micro-percussion, change by slow modulation, 125–130 BPM.
resolution.romanian-minimal: swung, sample-based, bass-led with the kick quieter than the bass, very long arrangements, 122–127 BPM.
resolution.tech-house: repeating bass-riff hook, vocal chops and house-style 8-bar builds, 124–128 BPM.

tags.meaning: In February 2020 Beatport split its Techno genre into two store categories; this one was first named "Techno (Peak Time / Driving / Hard)". After Hard Techno became its own category again in mid-2020, the label was used as "Techno (Peak Time / Driving)" on track pages (exact renaming date uncertain). Files bought since 2020 carry one of the two spellings in the genre field. It means "main-room techno with drive", typically 130–145 BPM.
tags.name: Techno (Peak Time / Driving)

resolution.acid-techno: a TB-303 resonant line for most of the track over straight techno drums, 130–150 BPM.
resolution.dark-techno: deep clean sub, sparse mids, no hooks and no drops, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: files from before mid-2020 with a distorted, rumbling kick at 148+ BPM ("/ Hard" in the old category name).
resolution.peak-time-techno: clean, punchy kick, riff hook, kick-less riser breakdown and brickwalled master, 134–142 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.
resolution.tribal-techno: dense, lightly swung hand-drum percussion as the main groove, 132–142 BPM.

tags.meaning: The second of Beatport's two techno categories from February 2020, for underground, non-festival techno: hypnotic, deep, raw, dubby, industrial or broken. It carries no tempo or sound definition beyond "not peak-time".
tags.name: Techno (Raw / Deep / Hypnotic)

resolution.ambient-techno: pad-led with the kick quieter than the pads, slow evolution, often 115–130 BPM.
resolution.broken-techno: kick leaves the quarter grid (skipped or offset kicks, snare off the backbeat) under dark techno textures, 130–142 BPM.
resolution.dark-techno: deep clean sub under sparse grey percussion and occasional reverb-washed stabs, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.dub-techno: chord stabs with fixed-interval feedback-delay echo trains over a hiss bed, 118–125 BPM.
resolution.hypnotic-techno: dense polyrhythmic percussion layers with odd-period loops and drones, no hooks, flat loudness, 130–136 BPM.
resolution.industrial-techno: sustained noise layers, long reverb tails on metallic percussion, distorted dry kick, 130–145 BPM.
resolution.minimal-techno: low element count, clicks and micro-percussion, kick-dominant, straight grid, 125–130 BPM.
resolution.raw-techno: saturated, lo-fi, jam-timed loops with a gritty kick, 130–137 BPM.

tags.meaning: Since Beatport's trance split on 23 May 2023 this category holds festival and classic trance with five sub-genres: Vocal Trance, Uplifting Trance, Tech-Trance, Progressive Trance and Hard Trance. Files from before the split carry plain "Trance". The underground side moved to tag-beatport-trance-raw.
tags.name: Trance (Main Floor) (Beatport)

resolution.hard-trance: bass that follows the chord roots under hoover or supersaw leads, harder kick, 142–150 BPM.
resolution.progressive-trance: pads, plucks and a rolling offbeat bass with warm, lifting breakdowns, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.tech-trance: rolling 1/16 bass with chord-root movement and tech stabs, harder drums, 138–142 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end (static sub or rumble) under a sustained trance lead; 2020s releases filed here although the drums are techno, 140–152 BPM.
resolution.uplifting-trance: rolling 1/16 bass, supersaw chords and long euphoric breakdowns, 136–140 BPM.
resolution.vocal-trance: full sung vocal song over trance drums and bass, 134–140 BPM.

tags.meaning: On 23 May 2023 Beatport split Trance into "Trance (Main Floor)" (with sub-genres such as Vocal, Uplifting, Tech, Progressive and Hard Trance) and this category for the underground side of the revival: hypnotic, deep and raw trance that often sits closer to techno than to festival trance. The exact sonic scope is not documented by Beatport; the resolution below is an assessment (uncertain).
tags.name: Trance (Raw / Deep / Hypnotic)

resolution.hypnotic-techno: odd-period percussion layers and drones with no lead melody, 130–136 BPM; files here when labels file hypnotic techno as trance.
resolution.progressive-psytrance: rolling psytrance bass (kick plus three bass notes per beat) with hypnotic layering, 134–140 BPM.
resolution.progressive-trance: pads, plucks and a rolling offbeat bass with warm, lifting breakdowns, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end (rumble or one-note sub) and straight techno hats under trance leads or arpeggios, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Berlin techno" and "Berghain" in mix and playlist titles started as names for the dark, dry, deep sound of Berghain and Ostgut Ton around 2008–2016. By the 2020s they are city and venue labels used for everything played in Berlin rooms, including hard techno, trance-techno and hard-bounce nights (for example "Hard Techno // Hard Trance // Hard Bounce" at M-BIA, 2026). The label says where, not what.
tags.name: Berlin Techno

resolution.dark-techno: deep clean sub under sparse grey percussion, no hooks and no drops, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab under a distorted kick, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: rumble tail under a distorted kick, hooks and riser breakdowns, 148–158 BPM.
resolution.hypnotic-techno: dense odd-period percussion layers and drones, flat loudness, 130–136 BPM.
resolution.industrial-techno: sustained noise layers and long reverb tails on metallic percussion, 130–140 BPM.
resolution.raw-techno: saturated, lo-fi, jam-timed loops with a gritty kick, 130–137 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Bounce" always points at an offbeat bass that alternates with the kick, but the word names at least five different scenes and one unrelated hip-hop genre. In 2020s German SoundCloud and club usage (GOTEC's "Bouncy Techno Set" titles, labels self-describing as "bounce" or "trance, bounce", flyers listing "Hard Bounce" as its own floor) it means hard-bounce. In UK usage "UK bounce" means donk; Scottish 1990s records are bouncy-techno; and "bounce music" in New Orleans is a hip-hop style with no offbeat techno bass at all.
tags.name: Bounce

resolution.bounce: New Orleans hip-hop: call-and-response chants over the Triggerman beat and a syncopated, not four-on-the-floor, kick around 95–105 BPM (planned note; tempo uncertain).
resolution.bouncy-techno: same bounce under a dry, moderately distorted kick with 1990s rave hooks and a band-limited 1990s master, 160–172 BPM.
resolution.donk: hollow, plucked, pipe-like offbeat stab in a hard-house frame with snare rolls and pop or happy-hardcore vocal samples, 150–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab under a distorted hard-techno kick with 1/16 hat rolls, riser breakdowns and a modern brickwalled master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hardbass: offbeat donk bass under a distorted kick in a minimal loop with chanted or rapped (often Russian) vocals, 155–170 BPM.
resolution.jumpstyle: bounce produced by a pitched kick tail or reverse bass rather than a separate bass stab, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.makina: offbeat stabs under a cleaner kick with a continuous 4–8-bar melodic synth or piano riff, 1990s Spanish production, 160–175 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Gabber" names the 1990s Rotterdam hardcore sound, but in 2020s titles it is also a loose word for any track with a very distorted kick above about 160 BPM, including fast hard techno, German Tekk and nostalgic edits.
tags.name: Gabber

resolution.bouncy-techno: distorted kick with a tuned offbeat bass stab and bright rave hooks, 1990s Scottish production, 160–172 BPM.
resolution.early-hardcore: breakbeat or early 4/4 hardcore with piano stabs and rave vocals, 1990s master, 165–185 BPM.
resolution.gabber: near-square clipped kick with no sub tail, hoover stabs, MC or sampled vocals, 175–190 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: rumble tail under the kick, techno hat grammar and riser breakdowns, 148–165 BPM.
resolution.mainstream-hardcore: Dutch hardcore kick with melodic leads and MC vocals in a modern master, 170–180 BPM.
resolution.tekk: dominant distorted kick with spoken quotes or bootleg snippets in simple loops, 160–180 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Groove" and "hard groove" in 2020s titles and label self-descriptions (for example Groove Street Berlin in the HEAT directory) point at percussion-led, swung techno. "Groovy" alone is also used for tech-house club tracks. The label names the feel, not the tempo.
tags.name: Groove / Hard Groove

resolution.hardgroove: swung, syncopated hand-drum percussion and chopped vocal shouts over a heavy but decaying kick, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.loop-techno: straight 909 percussion and filtered stab loops, clean kick, no swing, 134–142 BPM.
resolution.tech-house: repeating bass-line hook with vocal chops, swung house percussion and 8-bar builds, 124–128 BPM.
resolution.tribal-techno: dense, lightly swung hand-drum loops with a lighter kick, 132–142 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Hard dance" is an umbrella for the 140–160 BPM harder styles between techno and hardcore: hard house, hard trance, hardstyle and their offshoots, and in the 2020s also bounce. Beatport's "Hard Dance / Hardcore / Neo Rave" category and "harder styles" festival billing use it the same way.
tags.name: Hard Dance

resolution.hands-up: eurodance-style sung hook over an offbeat bass, cleaner kick, song form, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab under a distorted hard-techno kick with a modern master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-house: offbeat bass stab under a cleaner house kick with claps and hoovers, 145–150 BPM.
resolution.hard-trance: bass that follows the chord roots under hoover or supersaw leads with long breakdowns, 142–150 BPM.
resolution.hardstyle: pitched kick tail or reverse bass that follows the melody, euphoric breakdowns, 150–155 BPM.
resolution.jumpstyle: pitched kick tail producing the bounce, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.rawstyle: pitched, distorted kick tail with screech riffs, 152–158 BPM.

tags.meaning: Outside Beatport, "hard techno" in upload titles, playlist names and mix descriptions means any techno-room track above about 145 BPM. Since the late 2010s revival it is the default label for fast techno on SoundCloud, YouTube and TikTok; the IMS report 2025/26 lists "hard and industrial techno" among SoundCloud's top scenes. Under the label sit rumble techno, schranz edits, bounce, trance leads, German Tekk, pop remixes and groove.
tags.name: Hard Techno

resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab alternating with the kick, pitched hooks, modern master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: rumble tail under a distorted kick, 1/16 hat rolls, short hook, riser breakdowns, 148–158 BPM.
resolution.hardgroove: swung, syncopated hand-drum percussion and chopped vocal shouts over a punchy, decaying kick, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.hypertechno: sped-up pop vocal hook sung over a large part of a 2–4-minute track, 150–165 BPM.
resolution.industrial-techno: noise layers, metallic percussion with long reverb, no drops, 130–140 BPM.
resolution.schranz: dense, distorted percussion loops in constant motion over a dry kick, no vocals, no long kick-less sections, 150–165 BPM.
resolution.tekk: dominant distorted kick with spoken quotes or bootleg snippets in simple loops, often 165+ BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: static sub or rumble under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: In 2020s club billing ("Hard Techno // Hard Trance // Hard Bounce" at M-BIA, Berlin, January 2026) and on SoundCloud, "hard trance" names a revival mood rather than the 1990s German-Dutch genre. The textbook case: Marlon Hoffstadt's "It's That Time" (2023), released under the alias DJ Daddy Trance, is described by the artist as trance plus hard house, while Beatport files it under Hard Dance / Hardcore / Neo Rave at 147 BPM. Beatport itself still keeps "Hard Trance" as a sub-genre of Trance (Main Floor) for the classic sound (since the May 2023 trance split).
tags.name: Hard Trance

resolution.hands-up: eurodance-style sung hook over an offbeat bass at 140–150, song form, cleaner kick.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab under a distorted hard-techno kick with 1/16 hat rolls and a modern master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-house: fuller offbeat bass stab on every eighth offbeat under a cleaner house kick with claps on 2 and 4, hoover or trance stabs and vocal-sample hooks, 145–150 BPM. Most 2023–2025 "hard trance" revival hits resolve here.
resolution.hard-trance: the classic genre: bass that follows the chord roots (rolling 1/16 or offbeat trance bass), hoover or supersaw leads, 16–32-bar breakdown-build arcs, 140–150 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end (rumble or one-note sub) and straight techno hats under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: A spelling cluster that hides two unrelated scenes. French and UK free-party sound systems spell their music "tekno" and its fast melodic strand "hardtek"; German producers spell theirs "Tekk", "Tekkno" or "Hardtekk". The Wikipedia article on free tekno notes that the tekno and tekkno scenes are not connected. Platform tags, playlists and file names mix the spellings freely, so the label alone cannot tell them apart.
tags.name: Hardtek / Hardtekk / Tekk / Tekno

resolution.free-tekno: classic free-party tekno: kick–bass bounce under mental or acid riffs, lo-fi saturated master, jam structure, 160–180 BPM.
resolution.hardtek: French free-party hardtek: distorted kick with a tuned bass on every offbeat (kick–bass bounce), melodic or sampled hooks and breakbeat interludes, 175–195 BPM.
resolution.tekk: German Tekk: one dominant distorted kick, spoken quotes, film or meme audio and bootleg snippets in simple loops, no offbeat bounce and no break sections, 160–180 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Hypnotic" in mix titles, flyers and Beatport's "Raw / Deep / Hypnotic" category signals repetitive, slowly evolving music without big drops. It is used for several techno strands and for psychedelic crossovers.
tags.name: Hypnotic

resolution.dark-techno: deep clean sub under sparse grey percussion and occasional reverb-washed stabs, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.dub-techno: chord stabs with fixed-interval feedback-delay echo trains over a hiss bed, 118–125 BPM.
resolution.hypnotic-techno: dense odd-period percussion layers and drones, no hooks, flat loudness, 130–136 BPM.
resolution.minimal-techno: low element count, clicks and micro-percussion, kick-dominant straight grid, 125–130 BPM.
resolution.progressive-psytrance: one offbeat bass note per beat with a clean kick and slow, minimal change, 134–140 BPM.
resolution.psy-techno: psytrance bass onsets between the kicks and dense psychedelic FX over a techno kick, 138–148 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Industrial" on SoundCloud, YouTube mix titles and flyers is used for almost any dark, hard techno; the IMS report 2025/26 even groups "hard and industrial techno" as one of SoundCloud's top scenes. The genre industrial-techno is narrower: noise layers, metallic percussion, long reverb, no drops.
tags.name: Industrial

resolution.birmingham-techno: dry, flat, grey mix with short tails and EBM-tinged loops, 132–140 BPM.
resolution.dark-techno: deep clean sub and sparse quiet mids, no noise beds, 128–134 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: rumble tail under a distorted kick, hooks and riser breakdowns, 148–165 BPM.
resolution.industrial-techno: sustained noise layers with high mid-band spectral flatness, metallic percussion with long reverb tails, distorted dry kick, 130–145 BPM, no drop dramaturgy.
resolution.raw-techno: saturated, lo-fi, jam-timed loops with short tails, 130–137 BPM.

tags.meaning: YouTube and Spotify mixes titled "melodic techno" mix arpeggio-led techno with progressive house, afro house and organic house; Beatport's own category is called "Melodic House & Techno" for the same reason. In the 2020s faster trance-leaning tracks also appear under the label.
tags.name: Melodic Techno

resolution.afro-house: syncopated afro percussion and chants under melodic pads, 120–125 BPM.
resolution.melodic-techno: minor-key arpeggio lead over straight techno drums, wide pads and long cinematic breakdowns, 120–126 BPM.
resolution.organic-house: acoustic instrument lead over a soft kick and hand percussion, 108–120 BPM.
resolution.progressive-house: house-derived groove with swung percussion, major or uplifting chords and long builds, 122–128 BPM.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end under a sustained trance lead or supersaw with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Neo rave" was coined by the UK event Bang Face (founded 2003 in London, billed as a "Neo-Rave Explosion"); a 2020 compilation "The Definition Of Neorave" is an early reference point. On 18 April 2024 Beatport announced Neo Rave as a genre, "coined by BangFace", covering "the harder styles of dance music"; it now appears as a sub-genre inside the store category "Hard Dance / Hardcore / Neo Rave". It signals a 2020s hybrid of techno, trance and harder styles with 1990s rave references, not one drum and bass grammar.
tags.name: Neo Rave

resolution.early-hardcore: breakbeat foundation (snare off the quarter grid for most bars) with piano stabs, hoovers and rave vocals, 140–160 BPM; the "old skool rave" side of Bang Face.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass under a distorted hard-techno kick with a modern master, 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-house: offbeat bass stab under a cleaner house kick with claps, hoover or trance stabs and vocal-sample hooks, 145–155 BPM. Revival hits filed as Neo Rave (for example Marlon Hoffstadt aka DJ Daddy Trance, "It's That Time", 147 BPM) resolve here.
resolution.rave-techno: four-on-the-floor kick at 130–142 under 1–2-bar hoover or piano stab riffs with short breaks; a modern track built in this grammar with retro stabs.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end (rumble or one-note sub) under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: Beatport made "Psy-Techno" a sub-genre of Techno (Peak Time / Driving) on 27 January 2026; files bought since then can carry it in the genre field. Outside Beatport the word is used for any psychedelic, trippy techno and for psytrance played in techno rooms.
tags.name: Psy-Techno

resolution.hypnotic-techno: odd-period percussion layers and drones without psytrance bass, 130–136 BPM.
resolution.peak-time-techno: one-note or octave sub with a riff hook and riser breakdowns, a psychedelic FX layer only as colour, 134–142 BPM.
resolution.progressive-psytrance: one offbeat bass note per beat with a clean kick and slow, minimal change, 134–140 BPM.
resolution.psy-techno: psytrance bass onsets between the kicks under a heavier techno kick with techno hats and dense psychedelic FX, 138–148 BPM.
resolution.psytrance: short, clicky kick with three bass onsets per beat and several layered psychedelic leads, 140–148 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Rave" is used three ways: for the 1990–1993 European and UK rave records (hoovers, rave pianos, breakbeats), for 2020s tracks that quote that era, and as a mood word for anything fast, loud and euphoric. Event and playlist titles use it freely ("rave edit", "warehouse rave"). It never names one drum grammar.
tags.name: Rave

resolution.acid-techno: a TB-303 resonant line for most of the track over straight techno drums, 135–145 BPM.
resolution.early-hardcore: sampled breakbeats (snare off the quarter grid for most bars) with piano stabs, hoovers and rave vocals, 155–185 BPM.
resolution.hard-house: offbeat bass stab under a cleaner house kick with hoovers and vocal-sample hooks, 145–150 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: modern rumble kick, 1/16 hat rolls and riser breakdowns at 148–158 with a rave stab as hook.
resolution.rave-techno: four-on-the-floor kick at 130–142 under 1–2-bar hoover or rave-piano stab riffs with 4–8-bar breaks; 1990s master or a modern copy of it.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end under a sustained trance lead with chord changes, 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: "Schranz" names the late-1990s and 2000s German loop strand of hard techno, but in the 2020s it is also a popularity tag: the IMS Business Report 2025/26 counts an 83 % rise of schranz uploads on SoundCloud in 2025, the standout underground growth of the year. Many uploads tagged "schranz" or titled "(Schranz Edit)" are simply fast hard techno or German Tekk.
tags.name: Schranz

resolution.hard-techno: sustained rumble tail under the kick, a hook, and riser breakdowns of 16–32 bars at 148–165 BPM.
resolution.loop-techno: clean, punchy kick and 2–4 interlocking 909 and filtered stab loops at 134–142 BPM; the slower 1996–2006 ancestor.
resolution.schranz: dense, distorted, constantly moving mid-band percussion loops over a dry kick at 150–165 BPM, no vocals, no kick-less breakdowns longer than 8 bars.
resolution.tekk: dominant distorted kick with spoken quotes or bootleg snippets in simple loops, often 165+ BPM.

tags.meaning: A title suffix such as "(Techno Remix)", "(Hardtechno Edit)" or "(Sped Up)" says that a known song, usually pop, dance or schlager, was put over a techno kick. It describes how the track was made, not how it sounds; the result can be a song-length pop remix, a German Tekk bootleg, a club edit by a hard-techno producer or a bounce flip. The IMS report 2025/26 counts a 147 % rise of TikTok's #Techno hashtag, where such edits circulate.
tags.name: Techno Remix / Techno Edit

resolution.hard-bounce: the source melody over a tuned offbeat bass stab and distorted kick at 148–160 BPM.
resolution.hard-techno: a club edit: the source appears as a short vocal chop or melodic quote over a full hard-techno arrangement (rumble kick, riser breakdowns) at 148–158 BPM.
resolution.hypertechno: the original vocal hook is sung for a large part of a 2–4-minute track, pitched up, over a distorted techno kick at 150–165 BPM.
resolution.tekk: short bootlegged snippets and spoken quotes over a harsher, faster loop (often 165+ BPM) with a dominant distorted kick.
resolution.trance-techno: the source melody rebuilt as a sustained trance lead over chord changes and a techno sub at 140–152 BPM.

tags.meaning: Since about 2023, "trance" on SoundCloud, Spotify playlists and club flyers rarely means 1990s–2000s trance with a rolling bass and long euphoric breakdowns. In the German and Benelux SoundCloud label scene (many labels in the HEAT directory describe themselves as "trance, bounce") it signals any fast (140–160 BPM), euphoric, melody-carrying hard-dance or hard-techno track. SoundCloud's first Music Intelligence Report (2025) counted trance uploads up 29 %. The label says "there is a lead melody and it feels euphoric", not which drum and bass grammar sits underneath. GOTEC's "Trancy Techno Set" titles use the same meaning.
tags.name: Trance

resolution.hands-up: eurodance-style sung or pitched vocal hook over an offbeat bass at 140–150 with a cleaner kick; song form.
resolution.hard-bounce: tuned offbeat bass stab under a distorted hard-techno kick with 1/16 hat rolls and riser breakdowns, 148–160 BPM, modern brickwalled master.
resolution.hard-house: fuller offbeat bass on every eighth offbeat, house claps and hoover or trance stabs, 145–155 BPM; hooks often vocal samples; no rumble.
resolution.hard-trance: bass that follows the chord roots (rolling 1/16 or offbeat trance bass) under hoover or supersaw leads, 140–150 BPM, long breakdown-build arcs.
resolution.trance-techno: techno low end (continuous rumble or one-note sub) and straight 1/16 techno hats under a sustained lead of 8+ bars with chord changes; 140–152 BPM.
resolution.uplifting-trance: classic trance: rolling 1/16 bass at 136–140, long euphoric breakdowns with chord progressions, no techno kick distortion.
